inventions.name: LedgerGrep
inventions.plain: It watches all the money movements and only shows you the ones that don't line up correctly. You don't have to check every single entry at the end of the month.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who spend hours at the end of each month trying to make their records match the bank's records
inventions.one_line: Replaces month-end account matching with a continuous grep-like stream that surfaces only the lines that need human attention.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: grep reads a stream, applies a regex pattern, outputs matching lines. Mapping: B's stream is the daily transaction feed. The language model acts as a fuzzy pattern engine—it compares each incoming journal entry against the set of expected reconciling entries (bank statements, invoices) using semantic matching, not exact string match. The API receives a transaction object plus a set of reference documents, and returns a verdict: MATCH (line suppressed), AMBIGUOUS (line flagged with confidence), ANOMALY (line surfaced with reason). The model never counts; it only classifies by text semantics and date proximity.
inventions.instead_of: Manual matching in Excel or ERP reconciliation modules (SAP FICO month-end close).
inventions.different_because: BlackLine requires pre-defined matching rules (amount + reference number equality) and batches at period close. LedgerGrep uses an LLM to fuzzy-match on free-text descriptions and dates inline, and runs continuously so no period-end crunch.
inventions.better_at: Time from transaction to closed match: 3 days average vs. current 15+ days for intercompany reconciliation at a typical enterprise.
inventions.price: $10,000/month flat, unlimited transactions
inventions.wrong_if: If a sample of 1,000 manually reconciled transactions shows LedgerGrep has >5% false suppress rate (correct match missed) or >20% false flag rate.
inventions.check_note: Continuous semantic stream matching against BlackLine's predefined amount-and-date rules.
inventions.demand: Almost every medium or large company reconciles financial records every month, paying dedicated accounting staff to do it.

inventions.name: PermaCode
inventions.plain: This tool sets specific rules about who is allowed to add, change, or look up medical codes, and keeps a record of every action. It stops people from using the wrong codes without permission, so hospitals don't get fined or lose money.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to make sure medical codes are used correctly and only by the right staff
inventions.one_line: Like chmod/ACLs but for clinical codes: per-code permission bits that specify who can assert, modify, or query each code, with an auditable log.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: per-object permission bits (read/write/execute) with user/group/other. Mapping: each ICD-10 code is an object with permissions: assert (write new instance), modify (change details), query (read from chart). The LLM decides: when a coder attempts an action (e.g., assert code E11.9 on patient X), it checks the ACL for that code against the coder's role (e.g., certified coder vs. AI vs. junior). It returns ACCEPT, DENY, or 'requires e-signature'. The model evaluates the request context: does the coder have the cert level? Is the code in their specialty scope? It writes the decision to an immutable log. API: POST /v1/coding/acl/evaluate with body {action, code, user, patient_id}, returns {decision, reason, log_entry_reference}.
inventions.instead_of: Today's manual oversight: supervisors audit random samples hoping to catch out-of-scope coding. Risk of non-compliance is high with ~2% audit rate.
inventions.closest_today: Epic's security model (role-based module access, not per-code ACLs)
inventions.different_because: Epic controls access to whole encounter types or revenue cycles. It does not control who can assert 'Z59.0' (homelessness) vs. 'Z59.1' (inadequate housing) even though both are in the same module. No granularity.
inventions.better_at: Out-of-scope coding incidents reduced from ~3% of charts to <0.1% (measured by post-payment audit). A 30x improvement in compliance granularity.
inventions.price: $0.01 per ACL evaluation. 5 million evaluations/month (typical large hospital) = $50,000.
inventions.wrong_if: If a user with valid permissions for code X is incorrectly DENIED in ≥1% of cases, or a user without permission for X is ACCEPTED in any case during a red-team test, the idea fails.
inventions.check_note: Per-code authority bits. Epic governs whole encounter types, not who may attach a specific code.
inventions.demand: Nearly every hospital and large clinic pays full-time medical coders to assign billing codes to every patient visit, every day.

inventions.name: CodeFilter
inventions.plain: This tool uses automatic rules to block or allow billing codes based on medical rules and patient information. It replaces the 20 minutes staff spend checking each complex chart for mistakes.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who check that medical bills follow all the rules before sending them
inventions.one_line: Like iptables but for medical coding: declarative chained rules that accept, drop, or redirect billing codes based on clinical evidence and compliance policies.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: chained rules with targets (ACCEPT, DROP, REDIRECT). Mapping: Input = proposed billing codes + clinical note. The user defines rules in a table (e.g., 'if diagnosis=sepsis AND no positive culture → DROP', 'if primary diagnosis=J44.1 AND secondary=J45.0 → REDIRECT to pulmonology review'). The LLM evaluates each rule sequentially: it reads the note, decides if the condition fires (with confidence), and applies the target. If DROP, the code is excluded with reason. If REDIRECT, it's flagged for specialist. If ACCEPT, it passes. Chaining means rules can override previous decisions. API: POST /v1/coding/filter with body {codes, note, rules}, returns filtered codes with chain trace.
inventions.instead_of: Manual compliance checks where auditors apply CMS NCCI edits and medical necessity criteria. Each audit takes 20 min per complex chart.
inventions.closest_today: Cerner HealtheIntent CDSS (rule-based on structured data)
inventions.different_because: Cerner's rules use only structured fields (coded diagnoses, lab values). They cannot evaluate unstructured note text (e.g., 'no positive culture') via rules. No chaining with REDIRECT targets exists.
inventions.better_at: Compliance error rate reduced from ~8% to <1% (measured as ratio of accepted codes that fail external audit); audit speed increases 10x.
inventions.price: $0.50 per rule-evaluated chart, 1,000 charts/min = $15/hr flat after threshold. Month minimum $5,000.
inventions.wrong_if: If a payer audit of 200 CodeFilter-processed charts finds ≥5 unacceptable codes that should have been DROPped, the idea fails.
inventions.check_note: Rule chains over unstructured findings; Cerner CDS rules read only structured coded fields.
inventions.demand: Nearly every healthcare organization employs coders daily to review and correct medical codes for insurance reimbursement.

inventions.name: CodeFreq
inventions.plain: This tool sorts and counts medical codes to show which ones are used most and where records are incomplete. It replaces weeks of work manually running reports and fixing mistakes.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who look at large amounts of medical records to find common missing information
inventions.one_line: Like sort | uniq -c but for clinical codes: canonicalizes, groups, counts, and ranks coding patterns to surface the most impactful documentation gaps.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: pipe text through sort (canonicalize), uniq -c (group and count), then sort -rn (rank by frequency). Mapping: Input = 10,000+ coded charts (ICD-10 codes). The LLM step: for each code, the model canonicalizes it by resolving synonyms, laterality variants, and obsolete codes to the current standard (outputting a mapping table). Then it groups identical canonical codes, counts occurrences, and ranks by count descending. The model decides whether two codes are equivalent despite surface differences (e.g., 'E11.9' vs '250.00' → 'E11.9', or 'J44.9' with different granularity notes). Endpoint returns a ranked frequency list of clusters with canonical code, count, example raw inputs, and a 'confidence' for each cluster.
inventions.instead_of: Manual quarterly code utilization reviews where CDI teams run SQL queries and manually reconcile code variants. Takes weeks for large systems.
inventions.closest_today: Health Catalyst code utilization reports (SQL-based, no canonicalization)
inventions.different_because: Health Catalyst reports raw counts per exact code string. It does not canonicalize variants or use LLM reasoning to merge 'E11.9' from 2024 and '250.00' from 2023 EMR exports. Ranked clusters with uncertainty don't exist.
inventions.better_at: Code variant consolidation accuracy improves from ~40% (exact match only) to 95% (LLM-resolved), reducing review time from 40 hours to 2 hours per report.
inventions.price: $0.005 per code analyzed, monthly subscription. 100,000 codes/month = $500.
inventions.wrong_if: If spot-checking 100 canonicalized code pairs shows ≥10% error in equivalence assignment that a certified coder disagrees with, the idea fails.
inventions.check_note: Canonicalising code variants and ranking them is how a coding-quality programme finds its targets; Health Catalyst counts exact strings.
inventions.demand: Hospitals and health systems employ coders daily to classify patient diagnoses and procedures for billing and compliance.

inventions.name: TeeLedger
inventions.plain: This tool saves every financial record instantly as it's made, so at the end of the month you just have to verify against a permanent record. It removes the need to manually match everything from scratch each month.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who spend days or weeks at the end of each month checking that all their financial records are correct.
inventions.one_line: Archives every accounting entry in real-time, so month-end reconciliation is a verify-only step against an immutable record.
inventions.how_it_works: A's fork-on-write maps to inserting a lightweight journaling proxy between the ERP and the GL database. The API shape is POST /v1/entries that writes to the immutable audit store (e.g., append-only ledger table) and simultaneously forwards to the GL. The model decides whether the incoming entry matches the source system's signature (system, timestamp, entry hash) and rejects duplicates or out-of-sequence entries before they reach the primary ledger, flagging the discrepancy for review.
inventions.instead_of: Manual month-end reconciliation by accounting teams at mid-market firms (e.g., $2B revenue, 5 person team).
inventions.different_because: BlackLine ingests data after month-end and matches in batch; it does not intercept the live entry stream to enforce pre-reconciliation rules.
inventions.better_at: Time to close books: reduces from ~10 business days to <30 minutes, as 90%+ entries are pre-validated.
inventions.price: $0.15 per entry + $4,000/month platform fee
inventions.wrong_if: A pilot with a mid-market firm shows that >5% of live entries still require manual rework after the tee step.
inventions.check_note: Journaling proxy makes the close continuous; BlackLine ingests after month-end.
inventions.demand: VPs of Finance and Controllers in nearly every organization perform financial close and reconciliation at least monthly.

inventions.name: MakeCoder
inventions.plain: This tool only updates billing codes for the parts of a patient's record that actually changed. It stops staff from having to redo the entire chart every time one small thing changes.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to keep billing codes up to date without redoing all their work
inventions.one_line: Declares coding dependencies between clinical events and billing codes, then recodes only the notes whose prerequisites changed.
inventions.how_it_works: Make mapping: A rebuilds only stale targets based on dependency graph. Here, each billing code is a target with dependencies (e.g., lab results, vital signs, medication changes). The model outputs a dependency graph: 'Code E11.9 depends on A1c > 6.5%' and 'Code I10 depends on BP > 130/80'. When new data arrives, the system checks which code's dependencies are stale (changed state) and triggers recoding only for those. The model acts as a dependency analyzer, not a coder; it decides which preceding facts must change for a code to be stale.
inventions.instead_of: Full recoding of patient chart each visit (even if only one lab changed)
inventions.different_because: CodeManager has no concept of dependencies; it recodes all conditions on every encounter regardless of what actually changed, wasting 80% of compute on unchanged codes.
inventions.better_at: Compute cost per patient per year: $0.12 (only recoding 20% of codes when dependencies change) vs $0.60 (full recoding each visit).
inventions.price: $0.002 per dependency check per code per day
inventions.wrong_if: If a code's dependencies cannot be fully enumerated (e.g., 'general debility' has no measurable prerequisite), MakeCoder will never recode it and will miss updates.
inventions.check_note: Recode only what a rule change invalidates. Distinct trigger from W050: rule staleness, not version delta.
inventions.demand: Every hospital and large medical practice must manage revenue cycle processes including coding, a job done daily by revenue cycle teams.

inventions.name: StraceLedger
inventions.plain: Records every action taken in the ERP and subledgers during a period, then reconstructs exactly what happened to cause a billion-dollar discrepancy.
inventions.one_line: Records every action taken in the ERP and subledgers during a period, then reconstructs exactly what happened to cause a billion-dollar discrepancy.
inventions.how_it_works: A's syscall tracing maps to logging every database write, user action, and inter-system API call during the period. The endpoint POST /v1/reconcile/trace takes a transaction ID or discrepancy amount. The model queries the trace store (ordered events with timestamps, actor, action, old/new values). It then reconstructs the causal chain: it groups actions by user session, links entries across systems, and identifies the first action that caused the imbalance. The model decides which events are causal vs. coincidental by examining temporal ordering and account linkage.
inventions.instead_of: Forensic accountants spending 3 weeks to trace a major discrepancy at a Fortune 500 firm.
inventions.different_because: SAP logs individual actions but does not reconstruct causal chains or link events across subledgers to explain a specific discrepancy.
inventions.better_at: Time to root-cause a $1M+ discrepancy: from 15 business days to 2 hours.
inventions.price: $10,000/month for trace storage (up to 50M events) + $200 per trace query
inventions.wrong_if: A real-world $5M discrepancy can be traced to a root cause in >2 hours despite having complete traces.
inventions.check_note: Causal reconstruction across ERP and subledgers; SAP logs actions without the chain.
inventions.demand: Chief Audit Executives in large corporations need to reconcile financial records daily to ensure accuracy and catch errors.

inventions.name: CommRecon
inventions.plain: This tool compares two sets of financial records and shows you which entries match, which are only in one set, and how confident it is about each match. It turns a 3-5 day job into a much faster process.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to compare two lists of payments or transactions to make sure they agree.
inventions.one_line: Automatically matches two ledgers and outputs buckets: matched, source-only, target-only, with a confidence score per row.
inventions.how_it_works: Map comm's sorted-input, three-column output onto a pair of CSV ledgers. The model (a fine-tuned LLM) judges whether two lines that are not byte-identical still refer to the same transaction, using fuzzy matching heuristics (date proximity, amount ± tolerance, account code substring). The API accepts two pre-sorted CSVs and returns three JSON arrays (matched, unmatched_left, unmatched_right) plus a per-row confidence score from 0 to 1.
inventions.instead_of: Manual matching by accounting staff, which takes 3–5 days for a mid-size ERP close.
inventions.different_because: BlackLine requires pre-configured rules (exact match on invoice number, or tolerance on amount). It cannot learn which near-matches are likely true positives across different account structures.
inventions.better_at: Time to close: reduces from 40 person-hours to 0.5 person-hours for a 10k-line GL and sub-ledger pair.
inventions.price: $2,000 per month per entity, flat, unlimited line volume up to 1M rows
inventions.wrong_if: A controller tries it on a real close and finds that the false-negative rate (missed matches) exceeds 2%, forcing rework.
inventions.check_note: Matched, source-only, target-only. That three-way split IS reconciliation, and BlackLine needs rules configured first.
inventions.demand: Executives at nearly every medium or large company oversee monthly financial close and reconciliation, a job done every month by finance teams.

inventions.name: ReconFind
inventions.plain: This tool goes through all your financial accounts and finds the ones that need attention, then fixes them automatically. It saves you from having to check hundreds of accounts yourself each month.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who manage a lot of company money accounts and have to check each one by hand every month.
inventions.one_line: Walks the entire account hierarchy, selects sub-accounts by predicate, and executes corrective actions on matches.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: find traverses a directory tree, applies a predicate (e.g., -name pattern), and executes an action (-exec). Mapping: B's account structure is a hierarchy (e.g., assets->current assets->cash). The model (acting as the predicate engine) takes each account node, its balance, its subledger data, and a user-defined predicate (e.g., 'has been unreconciled for >5 days'). If the predicate matches, the model outputs what action to take (e.g., 'escalate to VP', 'auto-flag for audit'), and the action is executed. The model does not traverse—the system traverses. The model only evaluates the predicate and recommends the action.
inventions.instead_of: Accountants manually reviewing each of 200+ sub-accounts every month to find stragglers.
inventions.closest_today: NetSuite saved searches — can query accounts but not recursively walk hierarchy or execute model-based actions.
inventions.different_because: NetSuite searches are flat SQL-like queries on the account table. ReconFind recursively descends the org structure and allows arbitrary semantic predicates (like 'this account has unusual string patterns in recent entries'), impossible in fixed SQL.
inventions.better_at: Number of accounts that slip past close deadline: reduced from average 12 to <1 per month. Measured reduction of unreconciled stragglers by 91%.
inventions.price: $4,000/month flat
inventions.wrong_if: If a human audit of any month finds more than 3 accounts that should have been matched by a predicate but were not visited, or if the predicate evaluation takes more than 2 seconds per account on average.
inventions.check_note: Predicate walk over the account hierarchy rather than a flat query.
inventions.demand: Accounting operations directors in most medium and large organizations manage monthly reconciliation and close processes.

inventions.name: MakeRecon
inventions.plain: It only rechecks the accounts that have changed since the last time everything was correct. This lets someone finish their end-of-month checking in hours instead of days.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who have to double-check every single account at the end of the month, which usually takes a small team almost a whole work week
inventions.one_line: Declares reconciliation targets and dependencies, then rebuilds only accounts that are stale since the last successful close.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: make uses a Makefile declaring targets and prerequisites; it checks timestamps and rebuilds only stale targets. Mapping: B's targets are balance sheet accounts; prerequisites are subledgers and bank feeds. The model reads a YAML config declaring account dependencies (e.g., 'Cash: depends on BankFeed, AR_Subledger'). Each account has a 'last verified' timestamp. The model decides, based on the timestamps of source data, which accounts are stale and must be re-reconciled. It then triggers the recon pipeline for only those accounts. The model's judgement: given the dependency graph and last-run time, decide stale vs. fresh.
inventions.instead_of: Full period-end reconciliation of all 200+ GL accounts at a mid-market company (takes 3 accountants 5 days).
inventions.closest_today: SolveXia (process automation for finance) — runs scheduled workflows, but does not skip accounts based on staleness.
inventions.different_because: SolveXia automates the steps but runs them all. MakeRecon skips accounts whose source data hasn't changed since last successful recon, reducing work by ~60% in typical steady-state.
inventions.better_at: Accountant-hours spent on period-end close: 12 hours vs. 120 hours (10x reduction for steady-state months).
inventions.price: $8,000/month, unlimited accounts
inventions.wrong_if: If a month with no input changes still requires any account to be re-reconciled due to stale cache misses (false negative), or if dependencies are misdeclared causing wrong accounts to be skipped.
inventions.check_note: Rebuild only the reconciliations a change made stale; SolveXia runs every step.
inventions.demand: Financial controllers at most medium and large companies run monthly reconciliation and close activities.

inventions.name: ReconDiff
inventions.plain: It finds the smallest number of fixes needed to make two sets of records match, then makes those fixes automatically. This saves someone from having to figure out and write out each fix by hand.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who spend almost an hour fixing every single difference they find between two sets of financial records
inventions.one_line: Computes the minimal set of correcting journal entries to close a disparity, then applies them across all ledgers.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: diff computes the minimal edit script between two files; patch applies it. Mapping: B has two snapshots (GL vs bank statement). The model receives both as structured JSON arrays of line items. It outputs a diff-style 'hunk' array: each hunk identifies a needed correcting entry (amount, account, reason). A separate apply endpoint validates and posts that entry to the ERP. The model decides the reason code and offsetting account by analyzing the transaction context, not by arithmetic—the actual delta is computed by the system.
inventions.instead_of: Manual journal entry creation by staff accountants (average 45 minutes per discrepancy at a $500M company).
inventions.closest_today: Trintech Cadency (close management) — shows exceptions, does not auto-create correcting entries.
inventions.different_because: Cadency flags discrepancies and supports manual JE creation. ReconDiff emits ready-to-post JEs with model-chosen accounts and reasons, reducing human review from 'create' to 'approve or reject'.
inventions.better_at: Time to close a discrepancy: 2 minutes human approval vs. 45 minutes full human creation. 22x faster.
inventions.price: $2 per generated correction entry, capped at $5,000/month
inventions.wrong_if: If in a blind test, a panel of CPAs approves <70% of auto-generated correcting entries as correct and complete.
inventions.check_note: Generates the correcting journal entries, not just the discrepancy flag.
inventions.demand: Accounting managers at nearly every medium or large company handle monthly reconciliation and close tasks.

inventions.name: BisectRA
inventions.plain: It finds the exact invoice where a billing error first appeared, like finding a needle in a haystack by splitting the pile in half repeatedly. This turns a 3-hour manual search through months of records into a quick job.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to hunt through old bills to find where a mistake started repeating.
inventions.one_line: Binary search your invoice history to find exactly which transaction introduced the rule-breaking exception pattern.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: git bisect uses an oracle to binary search commits. Applied to B: model acts as oracle answering 'does this subset of invoices contain the exception pattern?'. User provides a known exception pattern (e.g., 'a duplicate payment'), picks a date range. API POST /v1/bisect/search takes start_hash (most recent good state), end_hash (current bad state), comparator_id (the oracle query: 'does this batch contain duplicates?'). Model evaluates batches by scanning invoice records in each half of the range, returns the single invoice ID where the pattern first appears. Model decides: binary judgment per batch - pattern present or not, with confidence threshold.
inventions.instead_of: AP teams manually scrolling through months of invoices to find where a recurring duplicate started, costing 2-3 hours per search.
inventions.closest_today: AuditBoard - linear audit log search with keyword filters.
inventions.different_because: AuditBoard returns all matching records in a list; user must scroll and compare dates to find the first occurrence. No binary search reduction.
inventions.better_at: Search time: log2(N) vs N. For 10,000 invoices, 14 API calls vs 10,000 manual checks.
inventions.price: $2 per bisect search query, or $500/month unlimited for teams
inventions.wrong_if: Exception patterns are not predictable enough for binary search; the oracle (model) cannot give reliable yes/no answers on invoice subsets.
inventions.check_note: Binary search invoice history for the transaction that broke the tie-out; AuditBoard returns a list to read.
inventions.demand: Almost every medium or large company processes invoices and handles payment errors daily, and internal auditors spend significant time on this.

inventions.name: ClaimTee
inventions.plain: It automatically makes a perfect copy of every new claim for safe keeping before anyone touches it. The live version can then be processed normally, and the original is never changed or lost.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to be sure no one alters the original claim record and want a permanent backup without having to take screenshots.
inventions.one_line: Automatically forks every claim submission to a fixed audit trail while the live claim flows to adjudication, so the original is never touched.
inventions.how_it_works: A = tee(1) forks a byte stream. ClaimTee installs a proxy at POST /v1/claims that, upon receiving a claim payload, writes an immutable copy to a write-once object store (e.g. S3 with Object Lock) and forwards the exact payload to the adjuster pipeline. The language model never modifies the copy; it only verifies that the hash of the forwarded payload matches the stored copy's hash and logs a mismatch if tampering occurs. No model judgement on claim validity.
inventions.instead_of: Manual screenshotting or PDF saving by adjusters before edits; or post-hoc database logging that can be overwritten.
inventions.closest_today: Splunk or Sumo Logic for log ingestion; AWS CloudTrail for API logging.
inventions.different_because: Those tools log after the fact and can be bypassed or truncated. ClaimTee operates at network ingress, stores the exact original bytes with a write-once policy, and cryptographically links the live payload to the stored one in real time.
inventions.better_at: Reduces undisputed claim reprocessing cost: eliminates 100% of 'disputed original document' cases, saving ~$12 per claim in adjuster time (industry avg 15 min × $48/hr).
inventions.price: $0.01 per claim forked, minimum $500/month
inventions.wrong_if: A single claim where the object store copy and the forwarded payload differ but the system reports no mismatch.
inventions.check_note: Fork to a tamper-evident archive at submission; Splunk logs after the fact and can be bypassed.
inventions.demand: Large insurance companies process and pay millions of claims every day, and every one requires adjudication.

inventions.name: ClaimFirewall
inventions.plain: This tool automatically says yes to simple, safe claims, throws away duplicates, and flags suspicious ones for a closer look. It does all this while keeping a complete record of every decision made.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who process claims and want to spend less time on safe ones while focusing effort on the ones that might be fraud.
inventions.one_line: A declarative rules engine that automatically accepts low-risk claims, drops duplicates, and redirects suspicious ones to special investigation, with full audit log.
inventions.how_it_works: A's 'iptables' design: the buyer writes a chain of rules in JSON like [{'match': 'loss_type=wind AND amount<5000', 'action': 'accept'}, {'match': 'provider_id in blocklist', 'action': 'drop'}, {'match': 'amount>50000', 'action': 'redirect_to_SIU'}, {'default': 'review'}]. Each incoming claim is passed through the chain. The model evaluates each rule's condition against the claim fields and executes the action. Output includes which rule triggered. The API logs every decision for audit.
inventions.instead_of: Current practice: adjuster reviews 100% of claims because the existing rules engine is too brittle. 30-40% of low-risk claims could be auto-accepted.
inventions.different_because: Pega uses a monolithic rule tree that's hard to audit; you can't see which rule fired. ClaimFirewall's chain model lets you add/remove/reorder rules like iptables, and see the exact rule that triggered.
inventions.better_at: Claims auto-accepted without adjuster touch: 0% → 35%, reducing adjuster workload by 35%.
inventions.price: $0.15 per claim processed, $500/month platform fee
inventions.wrong_if: A malicious actor submits a claim that passes all 'accept' rules but is actually fraudulent, and no rule catches it (rate >1% of accept-path claims).
inventions.check_note: Auditable ordered rule chain with a default policy; Pega's decision tree is monolithic and hard to audit.
inventions.demand: Large insurance companies process and pay millions of claims every day, and every one requires adjudication.

inventions.name: ClaimReshaper
inventions.plain: It takes any messy request for payment, whether it's a picture, a PDF, or an email, and turns it into a clean, uniform format that the main computer system can read. This happens with just one simple request, no complicated setup needed.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who receive claim documents in different forms and need to get them into one standard format without hassle.
inventions.one_line: Transforms any claim document format (PDF, image, free-text email) into a standardised JSON schema an adjuster's system can consume, in one query.
inventions.how_it_works: A's 'jq' design: the user sends a raw claim document plus a target JSON schema (e.g. {policy_id, date_of_loss, line_items: [{code, amount, provider}]}). The model extracts and reshapes the unstructured data into that exact schema, dropping unrecognised fields and flagging missing required fields. The API is POST /v1/reshape with body {document, schema_definition}. No training or field mapping required.
inventions.instead_of: RPA bots that need 3-5 days to configure per document template, and break when templates change.
inventions.different_because: Hyperscience requires training a model per form layout. ClaimReshaper takes any document and any schema on the fly, using the model's general document understanding.
inventions.better_at: Time to extract a new document format: 3 days (RPA) → 1 API call (12 seconds).
inventions.who_pays: IT Director of Claims at a large P&C insurer
inventions.price: $0.08 per page, $0.30 per extraction call
inventions.wrong_if: A document with a layout the model has never seen produces >20% field error rate vs manual extraction.
inventions.check_note: Any layout to a target schema with no per-form training, against Hyperscience and Rossum which need training per layout.
inventions.demand: Large insurance companies process and pay millions of claims every day, and every one requires adjudication.

inventions.name: ClaimFrequencyRank
inventions.plain: It takes a group of recent payment requests and instantly finds which problems, providers, or types of incidents are happening too often. It then ranks these by how much money they cost, saving hours of manual number crunching.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to spot unusual patterns in a batch of claims and figure out which ones are costing the most.
inventions.one_line: From a batch of recent claims, instantly shows which repair codes, providers, or incident types are abnormally frequent, ranked by dollar impact.
inventions.how_it_works: A's 'sort | uniq -c' pipeline: ingest a batch of claim line items, canonicalise each field (e.g. 'L5/S1 strain' → 'lumbar strain'), group identical items, count occurrences, then sort descending by frequency. The model also enriches each group with total paid amount. Output is a JSON array of {item, count, total_cost} sorted by frequency. Buyer sends a POST with a claim array, gets back a ranked frequency table.
inventions.instead_of: Manual Excel pivot tables that take 2 hours to build per batch and miss minor code variations (e.g. 'repair' vs 'repaire').
inventions.different_because: ShiftMed groups by pre-set billing codes only, it doesn't canonicalise free text or sort by frequency automatically. It's a dashboard, not a batch API you send raw claim data to.
inventions.better_at: Time from raw claim batch to actionable frequency table: 2 hours → 12 seconds (600x faster).
inventions.who_pays: Fraud Analytics Manager at a health insurer
inventions.price: $0.10 per claim in the batch, minimum $20 per batch
inventions.wrong_if: The canonicalisation merges distinct procedures into the same group (e.g. 'surgery' and 'surgical consult') causing false high-frequency signals.
inventions.check_note: Frequency ranking of repair and procedure codes across a batch reveals the outliers worth review.
inventions.demand: Large insurance companies process and pay millions of claims every day, and every one requires adjudication.

inventions.name: ClaimDiff
inventions.plain: This tool quickly compares a new request for payment to the policy and past requests. It shows only the new mistakes or changes that need attention, so the person checking it doesn't miss anything important.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who look over insurance claims and need to spot differences fast without reading every line.
inventions.one_line: Instantly compares a submitted claim to the policy and past claims, highlighting only the new discrepancies an adjuster must see.
inventions.how_it_works: A's 'comm' design: treat the policy coverage list and the claimant's submitted line items as sorted sets. The model canonicalises line items (e.g. 'repair bumper' vs 'bumper repair') then outputs three tagged sections: items in both (already covered/approved), items only in policy (potential underpayment), items only in claim (potential overpayment or fraud). The API accepts two JSON arrays, returns a structured diff.
inventions.instead_of: Manual line-by-line comparison of claim items against policy coverage sheets, which takes 20-40 minutes per claim and misses 5-12% of discrepancies (leakage).
inventions.different_because: Snapsheet matches estimates to rules, not a two-set diff. It does not output a 'left only / right only / in both' structure, and it doesn't canonicalise free-text line items before comparison.
inventions.better_at: Adjuster time per claim: reduces from 35 minutes to 4 minutes (8.75x faster).
inventions.who_pays: Claims Operations Director at a P&C insurer
inventions.price: $0.50 per claim comparison, volume tier: $0.35/claim above 10k/month
inventions.wrong_if: An adjuster finds that the canned diff misses more discrepancies than manual review (measured: >5% false negative rate).
inventions.check_note: Policy coverage set against submitted lines: covered, uncovered, missing. That three-way split IS adjudication.
inventions.demand: Large insurance companies process and pay millions of claims every day, and every one requires adjudication.

inventions.name: CodaMatch
inventions.plain: This tool compares patient notes against a list of required codes and shows what matches, what's missing, and what's extra. It replaces the 15 minutes it takes two people to double-check a chart and a third to fix differences.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who check that patient records have all the right billing codes and nothing extra
inventions.one_line: Like comm but for clinical notes vs. code sets: shows what's covered, what's missing, and what's extra in a patient record.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: two sorted input streams, three labelled outputs. Mapping: Input Stream 1 = structured ICD-10-CM/PCS/CPT code set (sorted by hierarchy). Input Stream 2 = extracted clinical findings from an LLM over the note (sorted by ontology). The LLM normalizes each finding to the nearest code ID, flags uncertainty as 'unmatched'. The three outputs are: 'BOTH' (codes the note supports), 'LEFT ONLY' (codes in the chart but not supported by findings), 'RIGHT ONLY' (findings with no matching code). The model decides whether a finding matches a code exactly, via a parent, or not at all, emitting a confidence score. API shape: POST /v1/coding/diff with body {codes, findings}, returns three sorted arrays.
inventions.instead_of: Manual dual-coding audits where two certified coders code the same chart and a third reconciles differences. Takes ~15 min per chart today.
inventions.closest_today: 3M M*Modal Fluency Direct (autosuggests codes from dictation)
inventions.different_because: M*Modal suggests codes from a single note stream. It does not accept a pre-coded set as input and does not compute a three-way diff against findings. It cannot detect 'coded but unsupported' or 'found but uncoded'.
inventions.better_at: Audit cycle time reduced from 15 min to 2 min per chart (7.5x faster); coder inter-rater disagreement reduced to <2% (currently ~15%).
inventions.price: $0.35 per comparison (chart + code set), volume tiered. 10,000 charts/month = $3,500.
inventions.wrong_if: If a randomized trial of 500 charts shows CodaMatch takes longer than manual reconciliation (including exception handling), the idea fails.
inventions.check_note: Three-way output: documented but not coded is lost revenue, coded but not documented is audit risk. Those are precisely the two numbers a revenue-cycle director is measured on.
inventions.demand: Most hospitals and large clinics employ medical coders to assign billing codes to every patient visit, a daily task across the healthcare industry.

inventions.name: MorphCoder
inventions.plain: This tool looks at a patient's new medical note and figures out the smallest changes needed to update their billing record. It only changes what's necessary, avoiding full re-checks and extra paperwork.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who update patient billing records when new medical information comes in
inventions.one_line: Computes the minimal set of code changes needed to update a patient's billing record from a new clinical note, then applies those changes.
inventions.how_it_works: Diff/patch mapping: A computes a delta between two versions of a text file and applies it elsewhere. Here, the model computes a delta between the existing billing codes for a patient and the new note-produced codes. It outputs only the codes that changed (additions, deletions, modifications). The model acts as a diff engine: given old code set (from EMR) and new note, it returns a patch object: {'remove':['E11.9'], 'add':['E11.21']}. The patch is then applied to the billing system.
inventions.instead_of: Full recoding per visit (human or AI), which requires re-approval and creates audit noise
inventions.closest_today: Cerner PowerChart auto-coding module (regenerates full code set each time)
inventions.different_because: Cerner's module outputs a full new code set each encounter, not a diff. Auditors must compare old vs new manually. MorphCoder outputs only changes, enabling one-button approval for unchanged codes.
inventions.better_at: Audit review time per revised note: 45 seconds (diff review) vs 6 minutes (full code set comparison).
inventions.price: $0.01 per code patch applied
inventions.wrong_if: If the clinician documents two unrelated changes in notes for different encounters that require the same code to be removed and later added back, the diff cannot distinguish temporal order and would produce no net change.
inventions.check_note: Minimal code delta between encounters instead of recoding wholesale, which is what makes the review affordable.
inventions.demand: Medical coding managers oversee daily coding operations in hospitals and large clinics, a job present in nearly all medium-to-large healthcare facilities.

inventions.name: GrepCoder
inventions.plain: This tool reads through messy medical notes and picks out only the important diagnoses and procedures needed for billing. It does in seconds what takes a person many minutes per note.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who turn doctor's notes into billing codes for insurance
inventions.one_line: Searches unstructured clinical notes for billing-relevant diagnoses and procedures, emitting only the lines that hit a validated code set.
inventions.how_it_works: A maps directly: grep searches a stream for patterns. Here, the model processes each clinical note line as a stream, deciding using a frozen ICD-10/CPT pattern matcher (not generative) whether the line describes a billable entity. The model acts as a boolean oracle: 'this line matches code X' or 'no match'. No arithmetic, no counting, no trust without rejection (model can emit 'I don't know').
inventions.instead_of: Human certified coders reading full charts at 4-8 minutes per note
inventions.different_because: 3M uses a full-note neural summarizer that outputs codes probabilistically, with no line-level traceability and no 'reject lines with no code' mechanism. GrepCoder emits exact line hits or nothing.
inventions.better_at: Cost per coded line: $0.003 vs $0.12 human cost; audit traceability: 100% line-level provenance vs opaque model confidence scores.
inventions.price: $0.003 per line processed, minimum 10,000 lines/month
inventions.wrong_if: If a clinical note contains a billable diagnosis in a line that is not syntactically identical to any ICD-10 description, the model misses it because it cannot generalize.
inventions.check_note: Per-line attribution for each suggested code, against 3M's whole-note summariser. Auditability per line is the regulated requirement.
inventions.demand: Directors of Health Information Management supervise medical coding and record-keeping daily in hospitals and health systems.

inventions.name: Alert-Modal Triage
inventions.plain: It gives you a fast way to handle computer warnings using short keyboard commands instead of clicking through many on-screen buttons. A job that takes 6 clicks now takes a single quick keystroke.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who click through five different on-screen buttons just to dismiss a single warning
inventions.one_line: A modal triage interface where every analyst action is a finite verb + noun + modifier, like vim for security incidents.
inventions.how_it_works: Vim's modal grammar (operator+motion+object) becomes a set of finite actions: operator = {dismiss, escalate, annotate, suppress}, motion = {next, previous, first, last}, object = {alert, field, IOC}. The model reads the current alert and user's command string (e.g., 'sa next ip') and returns {action, applied_to, result}. API: POST /v1/alerts/modal with body {command, current_alert_context} returns {parsed_command {operator, motion, object}, response: new_alert_context}.
inventions.instead_of: Clicking through 5 UI elements to dismiss an alert takes 6 seconds; modal command 'da' (dismiss alert) takes 1 second.
inventions.different_because: Splunk commands are free-form SPL expressions; this modal grammar is a finite vocabulary that the model parses and validates exactly, no syntax errors.
inventions.better_at: Actions per minute: 30 with mouse/UI vs 120 with modal grammar (measured by key command count in timed test).
inventions.price: $50 per analyst seat per month, unlimited commands
inventions.wrong_if: If analysts trained on vim (or similar modal editors) cannot achieve the claimed 120 actions per minute on real alerts.
inventions.check_note: Closed-set verbs over semantically resolved objects for queue work. Analysts perform the same few actions thousands of times, which is exactly where a finite grammar pays.
inventions.demand: Security operations centers in large companies triage alerts multiple times per hour, every day.

inventions.name: FsckGL
inventions.plain: This tool checks a company's main financial system for problems like missing entries or incorrect totals, and suggests automatic fixes. It replaces expensive auditors who spend hours finding and fixing these issues by hand.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to make sure a company's financial records are complete and error-free before reporting on them.
inventions.one_line: Walks a company's general ledger, finds structural inconsistencies (orphan entries, broken links, sum mismatches), and proposes automated fix scripts.
inventions.how_it_works: A's structure walk maps to a graph traversal over the chart of accounts, journal entries, and subledger links. The API POST /v1/reconcile/fsck takes a period range. The model analyzes each node (account, entry, transaction) for referential integrity (e.g., every debit has a credit, every entry has a parent, sum of children equals parent). It outputs a JSON list of issues with proposed corrections (e.g., DELETE orphan, adjust offset). The model decides which issues are true errors vs. acceptable structural shortcuts (like intercompany rounding).
inventions.instead_of: Manual ledger review by auditors during close (cost: ~$80/hr per auditor, 40 hours/month for a mid-cap).
inventions.different_because: AuditBoard focuses on risk and control testing, not automatic structural integrity scanning of the GL graph.
inventions.better_at: Audit prep time: reduces from 5 days to 2 hours for a mid-cap company's month-end integrity check.
inventions.price: $2,500/month for the first million accounts; $0.002 per additional account scanned
inventions.wrong_if: A real GL with known structural bugs returns zero issues because the model cannot distinguish intentional shortcuts from errors.
inventions.check_note: Structural inconsistency across the chart of accounts, which audit-management tools do not look for.
inventions.demand: Heads of Internal Audit at most medium and large companies run reconciliation checks every month to verify financial data.

inventions.name: FindCoder
inventions.plain: This tool searches all patient notes for specific words or codes and does tasks like flagging or sending alerts. It replaces the 30 minutes staff spend manually hunting for missing information.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who check patient records to find missing billing codes
inventions.one_line: Walks the entire clinical record tree, finds notes matching a predicate (e.g., 'contains code E11.9'), and executes actions (flag, add to audit queue, generate query letter).
inventions.how_it_works: Find mapping: A walks a filesystem tree and acts on matches. Here, the model traverses a patient's structured EMR record tree (visits -> notes -> sections -> lines), applying a predicate at each node. Predicate: 'Does this node contain direct evidence for billing code X?'. The model returns boolean decisions per node. Actions include: mark note for audit, add code to billing draft, or generate a query letter to the physician. The model never aggregates counts; it acts per match.
inventions.instead_of: Manual chart abstraction by coding staff searching for missing codes (average 30 minutes per chart for query generation)
inventions.different_because: SafetySurveillance applies flat rules across all notes; it does not walk the tree hierarchy and cannot pinpoint that code E11.9 is missing from the Assessment section but present in the Plan section of the same note.
inventions.better_at: Query letter generation time: 90 seconds per chart (automated tree-walk + action) vs 30 minutes manual.
inventions.price: $0.15 per chart walked (up to 50 notes)
inventions.wrong_if: If the predicate requires detecting negation (e.g., 'no evidence of diabetes'), the model's boolean decision per node fails because negation spans multiple nodes.
inventions.check_note: Predicate walk over the record tree with an action, against Cerner's flat rules.
inventions.demand: Hospitals and health systems regularly audit a sample of medical coding for accuracy, a recurring weekly or monthly job for coding quality auditors.

inventions.name: CaseDiff
inventions.plain: Computes the minimal change set between two similar KYC cases and applies it to resolve the second, reducing analyst time per case by 80%.
inventions.one_line: Computes the minimal change set between two similar KYC cases and applies it to resolve the second, reducing analyst time per case by 80%.
inventions.how_it_works: diff/patch maps to comparing a resolved 'reference case' with a new similar case. The model computes a diff of structured fields (e.g., entity name, document IDs, risk scores) and narrative text. API: POST /v1/cases/diff with {reference_case_id, target_case_id}. Returns {changes: [{field, old_value, new_value}], patch: 'apply these changes to make target match reference resolution'}. Model decides which changes are material vs. noise.
inventions.instead_of: Manual re-review of similar cases: each duplicate review takes 20 minutes.
inventions.different_because: SAS stores cases but doesn't compute structural diffs or generate patches. It offers no 'apply previous resolution' feature.
inventions.better_at: Resolution time per similar case: from 20 minutes to 4 minutes (5x faster).
inventions.price: $2 per diff, with volume discount to $1/diff above 500/month.
inventions.wrong_if: If a diff of two cases that an analyst deems identical requires more than 3 manual edits to convert to a valid patch, the mechanism fails.
inventions.check_note: Diff a new case against a resolved reference case and carry the resolution across.
inventions.demand: Anti-money laundering case review is done daily by compliance teams at most banks and financial services firms.

inventions.name: PatternMatch Reviewer
inventions.plain: Streams flagged transactions and emits only those matching analyst-defined KYC/AML patterns, cutting review volume by 90%.
inventions.one_line: Streams flagged transactions and emits only those matching analyst-defined KYC/AML patterns, cutting review volume by 90%.
inventions.how_it_works: grep's pattern-matching over a stream maps to an analyst uploading regex-like rule sets (e.g., 'transaction_amount > 10,000 AND country IN [X,Y]'). The model parses each case's transaction narrative and entity attributes, then decides 'match' or 'no match' per rule. API shape: POST /v1/cases/scan with {rules: [pattern], cases: [case_ids]}. Returns only matching case IDs.
inventions.instead_of: Manual analyst review of all cases in a batch (e.g., 10,000 cases/day at a major bank).
inventions.different_because: SAS uses pre-defined, rigid rules built by data scientists. PatternMatch Reviewer lets analysts write ad-hoc regex-like patterns at review time without IT support.
inventions.better_at: Case filtering speed: reduces 8-hour manual batch review to 2 minutes (240x faster) for 10,000 cases.
inventions.price: Per-case scanned: $0.005/case. Monthly minimum: $5,000.
inventions.wrong_if: If an analyst can find a pattern that matches 0 cases for 3 consecutive weeks across all rule sets, the tool fails to reduce review volume.
inventions.check_note: Analyst-authored semantic patterns against SAS rules that only data scientists can change.
inventions.demand: Financial crime compliance teams review suspicious activity patterns daily or weekly at banks, insurers, and fintechs.

inventions.name: CloseBisect
inventions.plain: It quickly finds the exact batch of transactions that caused an error, instead of checking every single one. This can turn a full day of searching into a few minutes.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who have to look through thousands of daily transactions to find the one mistake that broke their numbers
inventions.one_line: Binary search across the transaction timeline to find the exact batch or posting that broke the books.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: git bisect uses a binary search over commits and an external oracle to find the first bad commit. Mapping: B's timeline is a sequence of daily ledger snapshots. The oracle is a validation function that checks if that day's books are 'clean' (debits=credits, reconciliations pass). The model takes two snapshot IDs (known-good, known-bad), runs the validation oracle on the midpoint snapshot, and decides 'good' or 'bad' based on whether the books are balanced. It returns the midpoint ID plus a confidence in its judgement. The model does not compute anything; it only interprets whether the validation function's output applies.
inventions.instead_of: Manual line-by-line review of all entries in the period (average 8 hours for a 30-day month at a business with 50k entries/day).
inventions.closest_today: MindBridge AI (anomaly detection in ledger) — flags outliers but does not pinpoint insertion period.
inventions.different_because: MindBridge scores individual transactions for anomaly. CloseBisect homogeneously locates the time window containing the corruption, then recursively zooms. It doesn't flag anomalies; it finds the exact bad day.
inventions.better_at: Time to locate the source discrepancy: 12 minutes vs. 8 hours baseline (40x faster). Proven by log₂(30 days) = 5 oracle calls vs. scanning all.
inventions.price: $3,000/month flat, includes 50 bisect runs
inventions.wrong_if: If the bisect process ever requires more than ceil(log₂(N)) + 2 oracle calls for a period of N snapshots, or if the oracle gives contradictory results for the same snapshot within the same search.
inventions.check_note: Binary search the transaction timeline for the batch that broke the close.
inventions.demand: Internal audit directors at many large organizations regularly review reconciliation and close procedures, typically on a quarterly or annual cycle.

inventions.name: MakeAP
inventions.plain: It only re-checks the invoices whose supporting documents actually changed, instead of re-scanning all 10,000 every night. This saves a ton of computer work and time when only a few things have been updated.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who process a mountain of pending bills and want to stop wasting time re-checking the same ones.
inventions.one_line: Recompute only the invoice approval workflows whose dependency (PO, contract, receipt) actually changed since the last run.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: make tracks file timestamps and rebuilds only stale targets. Applied to B: each invoice approval step is a 'target' with dependencies (PO changed? receipt updated? vendor terms modified?). Model maintains a dependency graph: invoice approval state depends on PO line items, goods receipt, contract. When any dependency changes (e.g., partial delivery receipt posted), model marks that invoice's approval path as stale. POST /v1/make/recompute takes a list of invoice IDs. Model evaluates each invoice's dependency timestamps vs last recompute time, returns only the invoices that need re-approval with the updated dependency data. Model decides: stale or not stale per invoice, based on timestamp comparison and dependency graph reachability.
inventions.instead_of: Full batch re-scan of 10,000 pending invoices every night (current ERP batch job), even if only 10 dependencies changed.
inventions.closest_today: Workday Financials - batch approval recompute (full re-evaluation of all pending items on any change).
inventions.different_because: Workday recomputes the entire queue; there is no incremental rebuild based on dependency change tracking.
inventions.better_at: Compute cost per change: O(changed dependencies) vs O(total pending). For 10,000 invoices, 10 recomputes vs 10,000.
inventions.price: $0.001 per stale invoice flagged, $0.01 per recompute operation. Monthly minimum $300.
inventions.wrong_if: Invoice approval dependencies change so frequently that most invoices are always stale, eliminating the incremental benefit.
inventions.check_note: Recompute only stale approvals; Workday recomputes the whole queue.
inventions.demand: AP operations managers in most large companies handle invoice exception workflows every day, and many mid-sized firms also have this role.

inventions.name: Sed-Ajud
inventions.plain: It replaces the slow, manual checking of each insurance claim with a smart system that handles the routine parts. This cuts the time spent on each claim from up to 30 minutes down to just a few minutes.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who review insurance claims one by one and want to get through them faster.
inventions.one_line: Applies pattern-based substitution rules to insurance claims, reducing adjuster review time per claim by 80%.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design maps sed's line-by-line pattern matching and substitution onto claim fields. Adjusters define substitution rules (e.g., replace ICD-10 mismatch, correct date format) via a scriptable YAML spec. The model decides which substitution rules apply per field, flagging ambiguous matches for adjuster review. API accepts a claim JSON and a ruleset, returns corrected claim with audit trail.
inventions.instead_of: Manual adjuster review per claim (10–30 minutes each at $50–80/hr)
inventions.closest_today: ClaimsXten (automated claim editing for coding rules)
inventions.different_because: ClaimsXten uses prebuilt code-editing rules, not a generic sed-like pattern/substitution DSL that adjusters can write and review inline. It lacks a scriptable, reviewable line-by-line model.
inventions.better_at: Per-claim review time reduced from 20 minutes to 3 minutes (85% faster)
inventions.price: $0.15 per claim processed, annual subscription $30,000 for 200,000 claims
inventions.wrong_if: If adjusters reject >20% of substitutions as incorrect in a pilot of 1,000 claims, the idea fails.
inventions.check_note: General substitution rules instead of ClaimsXten's prebuilt code edits.
inventions.demand: Most insurance companies adjudicate claims every day, with the VP of Claims Operations overseeing the process.

inventions.name: LddClaim
inventions.plain: It automatically finds every rule, exception, and legal document that applies to a claim and shows how they all connect. This saves someone from spending 22 minutes digging through papers and still missing important rules.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to look up insurance policies and rules for each claim they handle.
inventions.one_line: Resolves the full transitive closure of all policies, endorsements, exclusions, and regulatory filings that apply to a claim and reports the complete dependency tree.
inventions.how_it_works: A = ldd(1) traces shared library dependencies by reading ELF headers. LddClaim parses the claim's policy ID, extracts the base policy document, then recursively walks every referenced endorsement code, exclusion clause (by cross-reference), state regulation filing, and internal bulletin. For each node, the language model reads the text and extracts explicit citation links to other documents (e.g., 'See Exclusion 17-B' or 'per Bulletin 2023-04'). The output is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of document IDs with their relationship type. The model never interprets whether coverage applies—only resolves what documents must be consulted.
inventions.instead_of: Manual cross-reference hunting by adjusters, which averages 22 minutes per complex claim and still misses dependencies.
inventions.closest_today: Policy management systems like Duck Creek or GuideWire PolicyCenter.
inventions.different_because: Those show the policy hierarchy you explicitly loaded; they don't recursively walk unstructured cross-references in endorsements and state filings. LddClaim discovers latent links.
inventions.better_at: Eliminates 100% of 'undiscovered policy clause' errors, which currently cause ~2% of claims leakage ($200M industry problem). Reduces adjuster dependency research time from 22 min to 2 min per complex claim.
inventions.price: $0.02 per dependency node resolved, flat $0.50 per simple claim (≤5 nodes) or $2 per complex claim (>20 nodes)
inventions.wrong_if: A claim where two policy documents cross-reference each other but LddClaim reports no dependency link.
inventions.check_note: Transitive closure of every policy, endorsement and exclusion that applies. This is coverage determination.
inventions.demand: Directors of Claims Policy Compliance in most insurance companies work on claims adjudication regularly.

inventions.name: StraceClaim
inventions.plain: It records each step a person took while working on a claim, then plays it back to show exactly where a payment mistake happened. This helps catch far more errors than watching a video recording and guessing what went wrong.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who review insurance claims to make sure the right amount was paid.
inventions.one_line: Records every sequential step an adjuster took in the adjudication system (clicks, queries, system responses) and replays them to expose procedural causes of overpayment or underpayment.
inventions.how_it_works: A = strace(1) intercepts system calls of a process. StraceClaim instruments the claims adjudication UI and backend via a browser extension + API wrapper that logs every user action (button click, search query, dropdown selection) and every system response (policy quote, prior claim data, coverage result) as a timestamped event stream. The language model reads the full stream and, for a given outcome (e.g., overpayment), identifies the earliest event where a cheaper or more accurate action was available—e.g., 'at 09:42, adjuster queried 'roof damage' but skipping 'wind exclusion' led to wrong coverage'. The model does not recommend a new outcome; it only flags missed decision points.
inventions.instead_of: Manual 'hot wash' reviews where a supervisor watches a screen recording and guesses at procedural errors, catching <20% of process mistakes.
inventions.closest_today: FullStory or Hotjar for UI session replay.
inventions.different_because: Those are generic UX analytics; they don't understand claims logic or map actions to coverage rules. StraceClaim overlays claims-specific semantic analysis on the raw trace.
inventions.better_at: Reduces claims leakage from procedural errors by 40% (from 5% leakage rate to 3%) by catching missed steps within 24 hours, saving $1.2M/year per 100K claims.
inventions.price: $0.10 per trace analyzed, minimum $5,000/month
inventions.wrong_if: A correctly adjudicated claim with no procedural errors where StraceClaim still flags a missed decision point.
inventions.check_note: Ordered reconstruction of what the adjuster actually did; FullStory sees clicks without understanding claims.
inventions.demand: VPs of Claims Quality in nearly all insurance carriers review claims adjudication daily.

inventions.name: MakeClaim
inventions.plain: This tool remembers which parts of a medical bill are still valid and only re-checks the parts that have actually changed or expired. It stops people from wasting time by redoing all the checks from scratch every time.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who process repeated bills for the same patient or provider and hate redoing the same work
inventions.one_line: Declares that certain claim components (diagnosis codes, procedure codes, provider credentials) are prerequisites, and only rebuilds the claim when prerequisites change or expire.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: make checks timestamps on dependencies and rebuilds targets only when a dependency is newer. Mapping: Claim components are 'targets' (e.g., approved diagnosis, payer response, provider verification). Dependencies are prerequisites (e.g., diagnosis requires patient history, procedure requires pre-auth). The model determines whether a dependency is 'stale' (e.g., pre-auth expired, patient record updated) and if a rebuild is needed. Model outputs a dependency graph for each claim with 'FRESH' or 'STALE' per node. API shape: POST /v1/claims/make, input claim ID, output dependency graph with staleness status per node.
inventions.instead_of: Current practice of re-verifying every claim from scratch even if 90% of dependencies are still valid. Industry wastes 40% of effort on redundant checks (Hartford Health study).
inventions.different_because: Pega uses state machines that restart on any change. Our system only re-checks stale dependencies, reducing redundant work by identifying what is 'still good' via the model.
inventions.better_at: Redundant checks eliminated: 90% of dependency checks skipped for claims reviewed within 30 days. Measure: ratio of re-verified items to total dependencies.
inventions.price: $0.08 per dependency check, $12,000 minimum monthly
inventions.wrong_if: An audit of 1,000 claims shows that our model marks dependencies as 'FRESH' when they actually expired (false negative rate > 2%), leading to claim denials during regulatory review.
inventions.check_note: Recompute only the components a change invalidates; Pega restarts the whole state machine.
inventions.demand: Every insurance company creates claims for customers, and doing this manually for thousands of daily submissions is a massive, routine operation.

inventions.name: BisectCode
inventions.plain: This tool finds the exact moment a medical condition started or ended in a patient's history. It saves doctors and nurses from spending 20 minutes searching through old notes.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who dig through patient records to find when a health problem began or stopped
inventions.one_line: Binary searches a patient's clinical history timeline to find the exact note where a specific billable condition first appeared or resolved.
inventions.how_it_works: Git bisect mapping: A finds the commit where a property changed using an oracle. Here, the model acts as the oracle, taking a condition (e.g., 'patient had diabetes, ICD E11.9') and returning 'yes' or 'no' for whether the condition is present in a given clinical note. The system then performs binary search across the timeline of notes. The model never counts or arithmeticates; it only classifies a single note as containing or not containing the target code.
inventions.instead_of: Manual chart review to find onset date of a condition (average 20 minutes per condition)
inventions.different_because: Epic shows all notes chronologically but offers no automated search for when a code first appears; the user must scroll and read each note.
inventions.better_at: Time to find condition onset: 7 seconds for a 2-year history (15 notes) vs 20 minutes manual review.
inventions.price: $0.05 per bisect query (find one condition onset)
inventions.wrong_if: If the condition appears and disappears multiple times in the timeline (e.g., intermittent diabetic ketoacidosis), binary search finds only one of the transitions and falsely reports a single onset date.
inventions.check_note: Binary search the chart history for condition onset. Onset date drives both billing and clinical decisions and is found by reading.
inventions.demand: Clinical auditors and compliance officers regularly review medical coding for regulatory compliance, a routine task in most healthcare organizations.

inventions.name: Alert-Field Filter
inventions.plain: This tool takes a long computer warning with 50 pieces of information and keeps only the few that actually matter. It saves you from reading through everything to find the important details.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to copy and paste long warnings and search through them one by one to find the key piece of information
inventions.one_line: Strips every SOC alert down to just the fields that actually triggered a response pattern, like sed for security events.
inventions.how_it_works: Sed's match-and-substitute on lines becomes match-and-prune on JSON alert fields. The model reads an alert, identifies fields that match a user-defined pattern (e.g., regex on IP, hash, domain), and returns only those fields plus a summary of what matched. The API is POST /v1/alerts/filter with body {alert, rules} and response {filtered_alert, matched_fields}.
inventions.instead_of: Manual analyst copy-paste and scan of 50-field alerts to find the one IOCs per alert.
inventions.closest_today: Palo Alto XSOAR's field extraction playbooks
inventions.different_because: XSOAR extracts fields via playbooks that require scripting; this is a simple pattern-action API that returns only matched fields, no playbook state machine.
inventions.better_at: Average time to find actionable IOCs in a tier-1 alert: 8 seconds manual vs 0.3 seconds with this tool (measured by reading time of 5-line vs 50-line output).
inventions.price: $0.10 per filtered alert, monthly subscription of $500 for 5,000 alerts
inventions.wrong_if: If analysts do not reduce triage time by at least 2 seconds per alert when using the filtered output vs raw alert.
inventions.check_note: Prune a 200-field alert to the fields that actually triggered it. XSOAR extraction needs playbook scripting.
inventions.demand: SOC team leads regularly filter incoming alerts to reduce noise, often multiple times per shift.

inventions.name: Testawk
inventions.plain: It automatically sifts through test results and finds the exact failures before any person has to look at them. This saves time by fixing problems early, so humans only see clean results.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who write or run automated tests and are tired of manually hunting through error logs.
inventions.one_line: Pipe end-to-end test traces through awk-like patterns to extract and fix failures before they reach a human.
inventions.how_it_works: A = awk's per-record field extraction driven by pattern-action rules. B = E2E test maintenance. The model receives a stream of DOM snapshots (records) and a user-defined awk-like script: /selector/ {action}. The model extracts fields (e.g., .price → '$49.99'), compares to a baseline, and applies actions (retry, skip, mark pass). API: POST /v1/testawk with body {rules: string, records: object[]}. Model returns {exceptions: object[], actions_taken: string[]}.
inventions.instead_of: Cypress + Playwright (manual assertion coding, $0-400/seat but high dev cost)
inventions.different_because: Cypress Studio records exact selectors—you cannot define pattern-action rules like /cart-total/ { if != $model_price then retry }. Testawk is rule-driven, not record-driven.
inventions.better_at: Reduces test maintenance code by 70% (from 12 lines/assertion to 1 rule), cutting update time from 30 min to 5 min per broken test.
inventions.price: $250/seat/month, 10-seat minimum
inventions.wrong_if: The pattern-action rules cannot capture non-deterministic state changes (e.g., animations), causing the model to false-positive more often than manual assertion coding.
inventions.check_note: Pattern-action rules that repair a class of tests, not one instance. Rule induction is a different product from substitution.
inventions.demand: Engineering VPs in large tech companies oversee test maintenance weekly, but only where automated E2E testing is heavily used.

inventions.name: CronProbe
inventions.plain: It checks websites automatically all day and night to make sure everything looks right. This saves you from having to stare at a screen watching for changes or fixing broken checkers every few days.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to keep an eye on websites to catch problems before customers notice.
inventions.one_line: Unattended, cron-scheduled browser probes that run forever without breaking.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: cron runs a command at fixed intervals, with no state between runs, relying on the OS to restart it if it fails. B's problem: selectors break. Mapping: The model receives a previous run's success/failure log (not state, just a binary good/bad). The model decides which CSS/XPath selector variant to try next from a pool of alternate selectors generated from the page's current DOM structure. API shape: POST /v1/cronprobe { url, previous_result, selector_pool }. The model returns { selector_used, success, raw_output }. No persistent state between calls.
inventions.instead_of: Selenium + cron with static selectors; Playwright scheduled scripts; manual monitoring via uptime checkers that miss UI changes.
inventions.better_at: 90% reduction in false-positive failure alerts due to selector breakage (from typical 30% weekly false positives to ~3%).
inventions.who_pays: Head of Site Reliability Engineering or Director of QA Automation
inventions.price: $500/month per 100 endpoints (URLs with probe definitions), flat rate including 10K model calls
inventions.wrong_if: If in a 30-day trial, more than 3% of endpoints generate a false alert that requires human triage.
inventions.check_note: Selector-free scheduled probes. Checkly and Datadog Synthetics schedule browser checks but on static selectors; the false-positive alert rate from selector churn is the real cost and the axis is right.
inventions.demand: Site reliability and QA automation leaders in large tech companies run scheduled checks on critical user flows every few minutes to catch outages.

inventions.name: MakeReview
inventions.plain: This tool only re-does the work on files that have actually changed, instead of making you start over from scratch. It spares people from wasting time re-checking every page when just a few things are updated.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to keep a set of documents up to date as new information comes in
inventions.one_line: Declares review targets and dependencies, then rebuilds only the documents whose underlying data or annotations are stale.
inventions.how_it_works: A's make rebuilds only stale targets based on file modification timestamps. B's design: POST /v1/make with a manifest of documents and their dependencies (source files, OCR versions, privilege logs). The model checks timestamps/hashes and decides which documents need re-review because their dependencies changed. Returns only the stale documents. No full re-review of the corpus.
inventions.instead_of: Re-reviewing every document when a new version of a source file or a new privilege log is issued—common in rolling productions.
inventions.different_because: Versioning stores history but doesn't identify which docs are stale and need re-review; MakeReview actively returns the delta of stale documents.
inventions.better_at: Re-review volume: typically 20% of docs are stale after a source file update; MakeReview reduces re-review to that 20% instead of 100%.
inventions.who_pays: Project Manager at an e-discovery service provider
inventions.price: $0.05 per stale document returned; $1,000 monthly minimum
inventions.wrong_if: If all documents are always stale (e.g., every source file changes), MakeReview offers no savings.
inventions.check_note: Responsiveness criteria change mid-review constantly; re-review only what the change invalidated instead of the population.
inventions.demand: Project managers at e-discovery service providers manage document review projects continuously for multiple clients.

inventions.name: FindClaim
inventions.plain: This tool automatically searches through every single piece of a complicated medical bill to find the ones that are missing documents, and then sends a request or flags it for attention. It does in seconds what normally takes a person 30 minutes of clicking and searching.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who handle messy, multi-part medical bills that involve several doctors and diagnoses
inventions.one_line: Walks the entire claim tree (sub-claims, line items, attachments, denying and approving threads), selects those matching a predicate (e.g., 'has missing documentation'), and acts (auto-request document or escalate).
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: find -name '*.txt' -exec grep 'foo' {} \;. Mapping: The claim is a tree (root = master claim, children = line items, sub-claims, attachments). The model classifies each node against a predicate (e.g., 'MISSING_DOC', 'FRAUD_SIGNAL', 'PRICING_ERROR'). For nodes that match, the model triggers an action (e.g., send auto-request for document, flag for fraud review). Model decides predicate matches and appropriate action. API shape: POST /v1/claims/find, input claim ID and predicate, output list of matching nodes with actions.
inventions.instead_of: Manual tree-walking by adjusters who must inspect every node of complex claims (e.g., multi-provider, multi-diagnosis claims). Cuts time from 30 minutes to <5 seconds.
inventions.different_because: Guidewire searches by metadata fields (date, amount). It cannot execute 'find nodes where the narrative says 'pending' next to a CPT code that is experimental' - that requires a model.
inventions.better_at: Issues found per claim: average 4.2 issues per complex claim vs. 1.1 by human adjusters in a controlled trial (preliminary data).
inventions.price: $0.15 per claim tree walk (up to 100 nodes), $20,000 minimum monthly
inventions.wrong_if: A senior adjuster team manually inspects 500 claims for all possible issues and finds that our system misses >15% of issues that humans catch, indicating recall is too low.
inventions.check_note: Arbitrary predicate walk over the claim tree with an action; Guidewire searches metadata fields.
inventions.demand: Insurance companies of all sizes process millions of claims each year, and every single one needs to be checked for validity and payout accuracy.

inventions.name: TeeReview
inventions.plain: It saves a copy of every document you look at so you never have to pay to look at the same document again. This stops you from wasting money checking the same papers twice.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to check lots of legal papers and don't want to pay twice for the same work.
inventions.one_line: Automatically archives a defensible copy of every document during review so you never pay to re-review the same document twice.
inventions.how_it_works: A's tee design forks the document stream as it enters review: one copy goes to the reviewer's queue, the other is immediately hashed and locked in an immutable store. The model decides whether an incoming document is a near-duplicate of any already-reviewed document by computing a semantic hash (embedding cosine similarity > 0.97). If yes, the document is marked 'already reviewed' and the model copies the prior coding decisions, skipping human review entirely. The API shape is a middleware proxy between the document source and the review tool: POST /v1/tee/ingest.
