inventions.instead_of: Relativity Assisted Coding, Brainspace near-duplicate detection (both still require human review of near-duplicate clusters and have no archival fork).
inventions.different_because: Relativity identifies near-duplicates but does not automatically fork and archive a reviewed copy; it still presents near-duplicates for human confirmation. TeeReview automatically skips human review on near-duplicates by asserting the prior coding is sufficient, and the fork guarantees you can prove the copy was never altered.
inventions.better_at: Documents per dollar: reduces per-document review cost by 40–60% for typical custodians where 30–50% of documents are near-duplicates, as measured in total human review hours per 100,000 documents.
inventions.who_pays: Director of E-Discovery at a law firm or corporate legal department
inventions.price: $0.15 per document ingested, with a monthly minimum of $1,000
inventions.wrong_if: If a controlled trial with 100,000 documents shows <15% reduction in human review hours, the idea fails because the near-duplicate rate is too low to justify the per-document fee.
inventions.check_note: A defensible archived copy forked at review time. Defensibility is a legal requirement, not a feature.
inventions.demand: Law firms and corporate legal departments hire staff or services to review documents in nearly all litigation and compliance matters.

inventions.name: LddDiscovery
inventions.plain: It finds every connection between documents, like which emails are part of the same conversation, and tells you if anything is missing before you start working. This saves you from hunting for missing pieces by hand.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who organize email chains and document sets and need to know if any parts are lost.
inventions.one_line: Resolves the full transitive closure of all document dependencies (attachments, threads, custodians) and reports what's missing before review starts.
inventions.how_it_works: A's ldd resolves dynamic library dependencies; LddDiscovery resolves document dependencies: for each document, it walks the email thread (Reply-To, References, In-Reply-To headers), attachment chain, and custodian graph to build a full dependency tree. The model decides if a document's dependency closure is 'complete' or 'missing' by comparing against a canonical list of expected documents (e.g., if the email thread has 7 messages but only 5 are in the production, the model flags the gap). The API is GET /v1/ldd/closure?document_id=, returning a JSON tree with nodes marked 'present' or 'missing' and a 'dependency score' from 0.0 to 1.0. The model uses a graph neural network trained on known complete email threads to predict missing nodes.
inventions.instead_of: Manual review of email threads to spot gaps (time-consuming and error-prone) and Relativity's Email Threading (which shows the thread but doesn't identify missing emails).
inventions.different_because: Relativity Email Threading groups messages by subject and time but does not compute a dependency closure or flag missing nodes. It assumes the thread is complete as given.
inventions.better_at: Recall of missing documents: manual review finds ~60% of gaps; LddDiscovery finds >95% in a test with 10,000 seeded missing emails, measured as F1 score on missing-document detection.
inventions.who_pays: E-Discovery Data Analyst or Forensic Collector
inventions.price: $200 per million documents analyzed, with a $2,000 minimum
inventions.wrong_if: If LddDiscovery fails to detect >80% of seeded missing emails in a test set of 5,000 emails from a known complete thread, the graph-based approach is insufficiently accurate.
inventions.check_note: Transitive closure of attachments, threads and references, which is what family-production completeness means. Email threading groups by subject.
inventions.demand: E-discovery data analysts and forensic collectors at law firms and corporations sift through digital records for lawsuits and investigations, a daily job in legal and compliance industries.

inventions.name: CommDocs
inventions.plain: This tool instantly shows which documents belong to just one person and which are shared by multiple people, without anyone having to read them. It saves reviewers from having to compare two lists side by side by hand.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to figure out what documents are unique to one person versus shared with others
inventions.one_line: Instantly finds documents unique to one custodian and common across custodians, no review needed.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: comm reads two sorted inputs and outputs three columns. Here, model tokenizes and hashes each document into a sorted embedding fingerprint. The model decides if two documents are semantically identical (match) or differ, then outputs three sets: docs in both custodian sets, docs only in set A, docs only in set B. API shape: POST /v1/commdocs with two arrays of doc IDs; response has 'both', 'left_only', 'right_only'.
inventions.instead_of: Manual reviewer comparing two custodians' document sets line by line.
inventions.closest_today: Relativity's compare sets function (string match only).
inventions.different_because: Relativity compares exact text or metadata fields, not semantic equivalence. It cannot group 'same meaning, different wording'.
inventions.better_at: Reduces cross-custodian review time by 95% (from hours to seconds).
inventions.price: $0.50 per 1,000 doc comparisons, annual commitment
inventions.wrong_if: A lawyer finds that semantically identical documents are routinely placed in 'left_only' due to embedding drift.
inventions.check_note: Unique to one custodian versus common across custodians, which is how privilege and completeness get argued.
inventions.demand: E-discovery project managers at law firms and service providers coordinate document review for most litigation and regulatory responses.

inventions.name: FreqRecon
inventions.plain: This tool looks through thousands of transaction records, finds patterns, and points out the unusual ones that need a closer look. It catches problems that people usually miss when scanning through long lists.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to scan through huge lists of transactions looking for mistakes or duplicates.
inventions.one_line: Groups and counts all lines in a ledger by canonicalised form, ranks anomalies by frequency, and flags the outliers for investigation.
inventions.how_it_works: Map sort|uniq -c to a pipeline that canonicalises each row (strip whitespace, normalise date, round amounts to 2 decimals), groups identical canonical rows, counts per group, sorts descending by count, and returns a ranked list. The model decides when to flag a group as suspicious: if count is < 5% of median group size or if the group contains an amount > 3 standard deviations from the mean. The API takes one CSV and outputs {canonical_form, count, rank, flag_reason}.
inventions.instead_of: Accountants manually scrolling through thousands of lines looking for duplicates, which misses 80% of anomalies.
inventions.different_because: Cadency manages tasks and approvals, it does not compute frequency distributions or flag statistical outliers in raw ledger data.
inventions.better_at: Anomaly detection recall: 90% vs ~20% for manual review, measured on a held-out dataset of 500 known data-entry errors from a Fortune 500 close.
inventions.price: $1,500 per month per entity
inventions.wrong_if: In a blind trial, the tool flags more than 10% of lines as anomalies, overwhelming the auditor with false positives.
inventions.check_note: Canonicalise then rank ledger lines to find the recurring shapes worth automating.
inventions.demand: Internal Audit Directors in regulated industries conduct reconciliation reviews every quarter to meet compliance requirements.

inventions.name: VimAP
inventions.plain: It lets you fix or copy parts of a bill using quick keyboard shortcuts instead of clicking through many menus. This makes changing a name or number on a bill feel as fast as using a text message.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who get tired of clicking through lots of menus just to fix one thing on a form
inventions.one_line: Edit invoices using modal keystrokes: press 'c' to change a field, 'd' to delete a line, 'y' to copy—with tab completion and undo.
inventions.how_it_works: Vim's modal grammar binds each AP operation to a key in normal mode (c = change, d = delete line, y = copy line). The model interprets keystrokes as operations on invoice objects. API: POST /v1/keystroke with {mode, key, target}. The model decides which invoice field is the 'object' (e.g., vendor name) and which 'motion' applies (e.g., 'w' for next word). Undo history maintained per invoice batch.
inventions.instead_of: Clerks clicking through 3 menus to change a vendor name on an invoice.
inventions.closest_today: Tipalti's manual correction UI is point-and-click only.
inventions.different_because: Tipalti has no keyboard-driven modal editing. VimAP lets power users do 15 edits/min vs. 5 edits/min with a mouse.
inventions.better_at: Edits per minute: 12 vs. 5 (2.4x faster) for experienced users.
inventions.price: $15/user/month.
inventions.wrong_if: If AP users cannot memorize >5 keystrokes, adoption <10% in beta despite 2x speed advantage, showing learning curve kills value.
inventions.check_note: Modal keystrokes for AP correction. Clerks repeat a handful of operations thousands of times, which is where a finite grammar pays.
inventions.demand: Many large companies have AP teams that handle invoice exceptions daily, but not all organizations have dedicated power users.

inventions.name: ClaimFsck
inventions.plain: It looks back at a finished claim, follows the steps the decision-maker took, and finds places where the rules were applied incorrectly. Then it suggests fixes before the payment goes out.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to double-check completed claims for logic errors and correct them before money is sent out.
inventions.one_line: Walks a resolved claim's decision tree, finds logical inconsistencies in coverage application, and proposes fixable repairs before payment.
inventions.how_it_works: A = fsck walks the file system's inode graph checking structural invariants (orphans, cross-links, bad ref counts). ClaimFsck walks the JSON decision graph produced by an adjuster (coverage nodes, denial reasons, benefit triggers) and checks structural rules: every denied node must have a policy clause cited; every partial payment must have an allocation formula; no circular policy dependency. The language model reads the graph edges and nodes, applies each rule, and outputs a list of node IDs with the rule violated. The model never decides claim outcome—only whether the graph's structure is self-consistent.
inventions.instead_of: Manual peer review of adjuster decisions, which catches ~30% of structural errors at $50/hr.
inventions.closest_today: Claims auditing platforms like ClaimVerify or FraudLabs Pro.
inventions.different_because: Those use keyword matching or fraud scores, not graph traversal of decision logic. ClaimFsck inspects the logical topology of the adjudication, not the content.
inventions.better_at: Reduces claims leakage by detecting structural errors at 3× the rate of manual audit (from 30% to 90% detection) for underwriting logic violations, saving ~$8 per audited claim.
inventions.price: $0.05 per claim audited, minimum $1,000/month
inventions.wrong_if: A claim with a known circular policy dependency that ClaimFsck reports as consistent.
inventions.check_note: Logical inconsistency in a resolved claim's own decision tree, which fraud scoring does not look at.
inventions.demand: Chief Claims Auditors in most large insurance companies audit claims adjudication on a regular basis.

inventions.name: AlertFind
inventions.plain: This tool searches through all your computer warnings and finds the ones that match what you describe in everyday words. Then it automatically handles those warnings, like assigning them to the right person to look at.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who sit at a computer all day looking at security warnings
inventions.one_line: Walks the entire alert database tree, selects alerts matching a natural-language predicate, and executes an action (assign/triage/escalate) on every match.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: find traverses the filesystem, applies a predicate, executes -exec. B's mapping: AlertFind takes a natural language query ('all critical AWS GuardDuty findings from us-east-1 in the last 24h that involve root credential usage'), walks the alert index by time-partitioned shards, and for each match executes 'assign to tier1-oncall' or 'tag as reviewed'. The model converts the NL query to a structured predicate and decides which action to execute based on context.
inventions.instead_of: Analysts manually selecting 50 alerts and clicking 'assign to analyst' in the SIEM UI, one by one or with clunky saved searches.
inventions.different_because: XSOAR rules are triggered per-alert, not bulk over a arbitrary set. AlertFind lets an analyst write 'find all alerts matching X and -exec escalate_to_incident' as a single command.
inventions.better_at: Time to bulk action 100 alerts: from 15 minutes (manual per-alert clicks) -> 10 seconds (one NL query).
inventions.price: $0.01 per alert matched + actioned; bulk discounts at 10k+.
inventions.wrong_if: If a user issues a bulk action and >1% of unintended alerts are matched (precision <99% on manual audit).
inventions.check_note: Bulk retroactive action over an arbitrary natural-language predicate. XSOAR triggers per alert as it arrives.
inventions.demand: SOC shift leads regularly search for related alerts across systems to find patterns.

inventions.name: FsckDiscovery
inventions.plain: It checks all your documents for mistakes like missing emails or wrong dates, and tells you how to fix them. You don't have to spend hours looking for errors yourself.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who deal with many files and papers and want to make sure nothing is missing or mixed up.
inventions.one_line: Scans the entire document population for logical inconsistencies (missing emails, orphaned attachments, contradictory metadata) and proposes a repair plan with a confidence score.
inventions.how_it_works: A's fsck walks a filesystem inode structure; FsckDiscovery walks the document relationship graph (email threads, parent-child attachments, conversation chains). The model acts as the 'fsck phase 2 checker': it traverses the graph, flags inconsistencies (e.g., an email with no sender, an attachment that references a parent that doesn't exist, a thread with a gap in the chain). For each inconsistency, it outputs a 'repair proposal' with a confidence score and a suggested action (delete, relink, flag for human). The API is POST /v1/fsck/scan, which returns a list of anomalies with JSON patches. The model uses a schema of document relationships extracted from the ESI load file and email threading metadata.
inventions.instead_of: Manual data validation (eyeballing load files) and Relativity's built-in load file validation (which only checks field types, not cross-document consistency).
inventions.different_because: Relativity's tool validates field-level constraints (e.g., date is a date), not cross-document graph consistency like 'every attachment must have a parent email'. FsckDiscovery checks that the email thread graph is connected and that all referenced documents exist.
inventions.better_at: Time to validate a 500,000-document production: manual takes 2–4 hours; FsckDiscovery does it in <2 minutes, with a 95% recall of real inconsistencies (measured against a gold-standard seeded corruption).
inventions.who_pays: E-Discovery Project Manager at a service provider
inventions.price: $500 per million documents scanned, with a per-project cap of $5,000
inventions.wrong_if: If FsckDiscovery cannot detect >80% of seeded inconsistencies in a 50,000-document test set with known injected errors, the approach fails because the model's graph traversal is insufficiently sensitive.
inventions.check_note: Population-level logical inconsistency: missing attachments, broken threads, gaps in a date range. Load-file validation checks fields.
inventions.demand: E-discovery service providers and corporate legal teams do document review for almost every lawsuit or regulatory investigation, often in large batches.

inventions.name: GrepDoc
inventions.plain: This tool quickly looks through millions of files to find the few that matter and throw away the rest. It saves people from having to pay expensive experts to read through every single page by hand.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to find important information in huge piles of documents
inventions.one_line: Searches millions of documents for responsive patterns and emits only the hits, cutting review volume by 90%.
inventions.how_it_works: A's line-by-line streaming grep becomes document-by-document semantic grep. POST /v1/search sends a query and document stream; the model decides for each document if it matches the query (binary classification), emitting only matching documents and their match scores. No ranking, no summary—just hit/no-hit.
inventions.instead_of: Manual first-pass review at $500/hr attorney rates; incumbent tools like Relativity require every document to be loaded and reviewed.
inventions.different_because: CAL ranks all documents and requires human training rounds; GrepDoc is a single-pass yes/no filter that streams results without any training or ranking interface.
inventions.better_at: Time to first responsive document: from hours (indexing + review) to seconds (streaming grep). Reduces review volume by 10x on a typical 500k-doc production.
inventions.who_pays: Director of Litigation Support at an AmLaw 200 firm
inventions.price: $0.50 per 1,000 documents processed; $5,000 minimum monthly commit
inventions.wrong_if: If a law firm can process 500k docs through Relativity faster than through this API including the grep decision time.
inventions.check_note: Per-document semantic match emitting only responsive documents. Relativity's active learning ranks the whole population and needs training rounds.
inventions.demand: Directors of litigation support at large law firms oversee document review technology and teams for major litigation matters.

inventions.name: GuideGuard
inventions.plain: GuideGuard takes the how-to guides your AI wrote and compares them against a simple checklist you already have for that process. It catches any steps the AI left out or got wrong, so you don't have to read every word yourself.
inventions.who_it_helps: Anyone who has to train new people or document how things get done around here
inventions.one_line: GuideGuard checks AI-written how-to guides against your actual process rules and flags every missing step or wrong detail before you share them.
inventions.tool_design: Analyze source text for violations of defined rules and report discrepancies, without executing the content.
inventions.task: Verify that AI-generated instructions or how-to guides for internal processes are complete and correct before sharing with new hires or teams.
inventions.how_it_works: The tool's design maps the process of 'linting' source code to the process of 'linting' procedural documents. The user provides a structured, machine-readable rule file (e.g., a checklist of required sections, mandatory warnings, required approvals). The model reads the AI-generated guide against these rules: it decides for each rule if the guide's content satisfies the rule's intent. It emits a report of rule violations, not a rewrite. The model's judgment: does this sentence or paragraph fulfill the requirement of rule #3 or not?
inventions.works_alone: On day one, a user uploads an AI-generated process guide and a rules checklist; GuideGuard returns a list of missing steps, wrong instructions, and non-compliant warnings.
inventions.instead_of: The current practice of a human training manager or ops lead manually reading every AI-generated SOP word-for-word against a checklist.
inventions.closest_today: Grammarly Business or Acrolinx for enterprise content compliance.
inventions.different_because: Those tools check grammar, brand voice, and style. They have no mechanism to verify procedural completeness against a structured rule set for a business process. They can't tell you the AI left out the 'escalate to supervisor' step.
inventions.better_at: Completeness verification time: from 15 minutes of human reading per guide to <30 seconds of automated rule-checking. Human effort drops 95%.
inventions.who_pays: Director of Training, VP of Operations, or Head of Process Excellence
inventions.price: $99/month per workspace (up to 5 users, 50 verifications/month); $499/month for teams (unlimited verifications, custom rule sets).
inventions.first_week: First week: A training manager at a mid-size bank sends the AI-written 'New Account Opening' guide plus the bank's 40-step compliance checklist. GuideGuard flags 11 missing steps and 3 warnings that contradict bank policy. The manager fixes only those spots, saving 6 hours of manual review.
inventions.wrong_if: If users find that the rule violations reported are mostly false positives (e.g., the model calls a valid step 'missing' because of phrasing) and that manual re-check takes as long as reading the guide from scratch, the idea fails.
inventions.demand: Training, operations, and process teams in large companies check internal how-to guides and instructions for errors and missing steps, several times per week.

inventions.name: FreqDocs
inventions.plain: This tool groups together nearly identical documents, counts how many times each version appears, and puts the most common ones first. It saves teams from having to sort and count similar pages by hand.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have a lot of repeat or similar documents and want to start with the most common ones
inventions.one_line: Groups near-duplicate documents, counts them, and ranks by frequency so you review the commonest first.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: sort|uniq -c canonicalizes, groups, counts, then sorts by count. Model canonicalizes each doc into a fixed-length semantic hash (embedding + clustering). Model decides which hash bucket a doc falls into, increments a counter per bucket, then sorts buckets by count descending. API shape: POST /v1/freqdocs with doc list; response: 'buckets' with count and representative doc.
inventions.instead_of: Manual grouping and counting of near-duplicates by a review team.
inventions.closest_today: Everlaw's near-duplicate detection (groups but does not rank by frequency).
inventions.different_because: Everlaw shows groups but does not sort groups by size; reviewers cannot prioritize the most common variant.
inventions.better_at: Reduces documents needed to read to reach 90% coverage by 80% (from 10,000 to 2,000).
inventions.price: $0.20 per 1,000 docs clustered, $1,000 minimum monthly
inventions.wrong_if: A test set of 100 distinct documents is grouped into 1 bucket, proving poor discrimination.
inventions.check_note: Rank near-duplicate groups by size; Everlaw shows the groups but not which ones are worth attacking first.
inventions.demand: Operations directors at e-discovery providers and law firms manage document review workflows for many simultaneous cases.

inventions.name: KYCDeptree
inventions.plain: It automatically finds every person, document, and warning linked to a financial background check, so you see all connections at once. This saves workers from spending 20 minutes clicking through five or more separate screens to find hidden owners.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to find all the people and companies tied to a single financial case.
inventions.one_line: Resolves every linked entity, document, and alert in a KYC/AML case, so analysts see the full web of related parties without manual lookup.
inventions.how_it_works: A's ldd resolves library dependencies recursively. Here, the model takes the initial customer entity and follows all relationships in the bank's graph database (accounts, transactions, linked parties, ultimate beneficial owners). It builds a dependency tree: 'Customer A -> Account B -> Joint owner C -> Director D (PEP) -> Company E.' The model flags if any node in the tree has a negative AML signal (sanction, adverse media).
inventions.instead_of: Analysts manually clicking through 5+ screens to find UBOs, taking 20 minutes per case.
inventions.closest_today: WorldCheck (entity screening, but not relationship graph traversal)
inventions.different_because: WorldCheck screens a single entity against lists. KYCDeptree traverses a graph of entities (customer, accounts, directors) that are already in the bank's system, not external lists.
inventions.better_at: Time to identify all related entities: 10 seconds vs. 20 minutes. Measured via task completion time.
inventions.price: $0.20 per dependency tree (or $2,000/month flat for unlimited)
inventions.wrong_if: In a pilot, the dependency tree misses a beneficial owner who is linked via a non-obvious path (e.g., through a trust), leading to a regulatory penalty.
inventions.check_note: Transitive closure of linked entities, documents and alerts. This is beneficial-ownership chasing, and WorldCheck screens one entity at a time.
inventions.demand: AML investigation analysts in banks and financial services review customer cases daily to check for money laundering.

inventions.name: AlertRank
inventions.plain: It organizes and ranks alerts by how often they happen, so you can work on the most common problems first. This saves people from having to guess which alerts to handle by gut feeling.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who get lots of alerts and need to know which ones to focus on without guessing
inventions.one_line: Canonicalises, groups, and ranks AML alerts by frequency so analysts work the most common patterns first.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: sort | uniq -c canonicalises lines, groups identical ones, counts them, and outputs frequency-ranked. Mapping: each incoming alert is canonicalised by the model into a standard 'pattern signature' (e.g., 'high-value wire to sanctioned country >$10K'). The model groups alerts with the same signature, counts them, and returns a sorted list by count descending. The API takes a batch of raw alerts and returns a frequency table with pattern signatures and counts.
inventions.instead_of: Analysts manually categorising and prioritising alerts by gut feel
inventions.different_because: LexisNexis groups alerts by entity name only, not by behavioural pattern; it cannot aggregate 'multiple small wires to shell companies' as one pattern.
inventions.better_at: Time to identify top 3 alert patterns: from 4 hours to 15 minutes (16x faster).
inventions.price: Per-alert-processed: $0.001/alert, minimum 1M alerts/month
inventions.wrong_if: If the model's canonicalisation produces too many unique patterns (no grouping) or fails to catch meaningful patterns
inventions.check_note: Group alerts by behavioural shape rather than entity name, which is what makes the top offenders visible.
inventions.demand: Banks and financial firms review and rank alerts every day to detect money laundering.

inventions.name: CaseCompare
inventions.plain: It sorts cases into groups like 'already matched,' 'new,' and 'closed,' so you only have to look at what actually changed. This saves someone from rereading every single case from scratch every day.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who review cases every day and don't want to re-check things that haven't changed
inventions.one_line: Automatically splits AML cases into confirmed matches, new alerts, and closed items so analysts only review what changed.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: comm takes two sorted inputs and emits three streams (common, left-only, right-only). Mapping: B's 'yesterday's case state' and 'today's alert feed' are the two sorted lists. The model tokenises each alert into a canonical representation (entity name, jurisdiction, risk score) and decides if it is 'same' (match), 'new' (left-only), or 'resolved' (right-only). The API accepts two arrays and returns a JSON object with three keys: common, left_only, right_only.
inventions.instead_of: Manual analyst review of every case from scratch each day
inventions.different_because: ComplyAdvantage shows a feed of all alerts without a structured diff; analysts must mentally track which alerts are new or closed.
inventions.better_at: Analyst hours per case: reduces from 45 min/case to 12 min/case (3.75x improvement) by eliminating re-review of unchanged alerts.
inventions.price: Per-case-per-month: $0.50/case/month, minimum 10,000 cases
inventions.wrong_if: If analysts do not save time because the diff output is too noisy or misses true matches
inventions.check_note: Confirmed, new, cleared. LexisNexis groups by entity name, not behaviour.
inventions.demand: Banks and financial firms compare cases manually every day to link suspicious activity.

inventions.name: FindCase
inventions.plain: It searches through a big list of cases, finds the ones that match what you're looking for, and then automatically does something with them, like sending them to a manager. This saves someone from spending hours flipping through a thousand records to find old ones.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who need to find and act on specific cases from a huge pile without looking at each one manually
inventions.one_line: Walks the entire case database, selects records by predicate (e.g., 'all cases older than 30 days with no action'), and executes an action (e.g., 'escalate to manager') on matches.
inventions.how_it_works: find maps to recursive case traversal. Analyst specifies path (e.g., '/cases/2023/*'), predicate (e.g., 'status=open AND days_since_last_action>30'), and action (e.g., 'set_priority=high'). API: POST /v1/cases/find with {path, predicate, action}. Model evaluates each case against predicate and returns action results. Decides match/no-match per case.
inventions.instead_of: Manual review of 1,000 cases to find stale ones (4 hours).
inventions.different_because: SAS search returns a list but doesn't walk subdirectories or execute actions on matches.
inventions.better_at: Stale case identification and action: 4 hours to 30 seconds (480x faster).
inventions.price: $0.01 per case traversed. Monthly minimum $200.
inventions.wrong_if: If findCase traverses 10,000 cases but the model misclassifies more than 1% (100) as matches when they aren't, the action fails.
inventions.check_note: Predicate walk over the case store with an action.
inventions.demand: AML operations managers search for related cases daily when reviewing alerts.

inventions.name: RecModal
inventions.plain: A modal keyboard interface where one key chooses the operation (match/flag/unmatch/split), another chooses the scope (line/page/account), and a third chooses the object (transaction/header/footnote).
inventions.one_line: A modal keyboard interface where one key chooses the operation (match/flag/unmatch/split), another chooses the scope (line/page/account), and a third chooses the object (transaction/header/footnote).
inventions.how_it_works: vim's operator+motion+object. Operator keys: 'm' (match to counterparty line), 'f' (flag for review), 'u' (unmatch pair), 's' (split line into two). Motion keys: 'l' (next line), 'p' (next page), 'a' (next account). Object keys: 't' (transaction), 'h' (header metadata), 'n' (nota bene). Model maintains a stack of actions and a cursor position. Never lift hands from keyboard; no mouse, no dropdowns.
inventions.instead_of: Mouse-driven reconciliation in BlackLine or FloQast: 14 clicks per unmatched transaction versus 3 keystrokes
inventions.closest_today: Vim keybindings in source code editors (VS Code Vim extension)
inventions.different_because: No editor applies modal grammar to structured financial data. The motions and objects are specific to ledger structure, not to text lines.
inventions.better_at: Actions per minute on reconciliation tasks: 120 (modal) vs 22 (mouse+keyboard); measured in controlled trials with 10 accountants
inventions.price: $15/user/month for desktop app
inventions.wrong_if: If a major ERP vendor (SAP/Oracle) adds keyboard-only modal navigation to their reconciliation module.
inventions.check_note: Modal grammar for high-volume matching work, which is thousands of identical decisions a day.
inventions.demand: Month-end reconciliation is done monthly by senior accountants at virtually all mid-to-large companies.

inventions.name: IptablesRecon
inventions.plain: This tool sets up clear rules for what happens to each transaction—accept it, reject it, or send it for review—and automatically handles anything that doesn't fit the rules. It replaces confusing rule lists that are hard to understand or check.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to set up automatic rules for handling financial entries but want to know exactly what rule did what.
inventions.one_line: Chained rule tables that ACCEPT, DROP, or REDIRECT journal lines into exception workflows, with a default-deny policy for unresolved lines.
inventions.how_it_works: Map iptables' chain-of-rules with default policy to a reconciliation pipeline. Each rule is a predicate (e.g., 'match amount > $10k AND account = 4010') with an action: ACCEPT (auto-match), DROP (flag for manual review), REDIRECT (send to a different sub-ledger). The model evaluates each line against the rules in order; the first match wins. The API accepts a JSON array of rules (ordered) and a CSV of lines, and returns the action applied per line plus the rule ID that matched.
inventions.instead_of: Unstructured rule lists in black-box reconciliation engines, where the matching behaviour is opaque and auditing which rule fired requires tracing logs.
inventions.different_because: BlackLine rules are unordered; if two rules can fire, which one wins is undefined or requires priority numbers that users misconfigure. IptablesRecon enforces strict priority by chain position, visible to the auditor in the rule JSON.
inventions.better_at: Auditability: time to determine why a line was matched or not is 5 seconds (read chain) vs 30 minutes (trace through ambiguous rules).
inventions.price: $1,200 per month per chain (one chain = one pair of ledgers)
inventions.wrong_if: A complex matching scenario requires a rule that depends on the outcome of a previous rule (statefulness), but the chain model cannot express this, forcing duplicate rules.
inventions.check_note: Ordered chains with a default policy; BlackLine's rules are unordered so two matching rules are ambiguous.
inventions.demand: Finance Systems Managers in large companies automate reconciliation processes quarterly to support accounting teams.

inventions.name: FindMismatch
inventions.plain: It looks at every single line on every invoice in a batch, but only flags the ones that match a problem you defined. This stops you from manually eyeballing thousands of lines that are perfectly fine.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to check every line item on invoices, even when most of them are from trusted vendors.
inventions.one_line: Walk every invoice line in a batch, apply your chosen predicate, and auto-escalate only the matches.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: find walks a directory tree, applies a predicate (-name, -type), executes action on matches. Applied to B: model walks a flat or hierarchical invoice batch (directory = vendor > PO > line items). User provides predicate as natural language or structured query (e.g., 'tax_code_mismatch AND amount > $5k'). POST /v1/find/escalate takes root_batch_id, predicate, action (move to exception queue, send alert to manager). Model evaluates each 'node' (batch, vendor, invoice, line item) against predicate, stops walking when predicate is false for parent (prunes tree). Returns matched nodes with execution result. Model decides: does this node (any granularity) satisfy the predicate? If yes, execute action and optionally recurse deeper.
inventions.instead_of: Current 'scan all line items' approach that checks every row even when whole vendor batches are clean, wasting 70% of manual review effort.
inventions.closest_today: Coupa - batch exception rules applied uniformly to every line, no hierarchical pruning.
inventions.different_because: Coupa evaluates every line independently; it cannot prune an entire vendor subtree when the batch-level predicate fails.
inventions.better_at: Lines reviewed per batch: pruned average 300 vs unpruned 1,000 (for batches with 30% clean vendors).
inventions.price: $0.005 per invoice node evaluated, capped at $1 per full batch walk. Monthly volume discount below $0.003/node.
inventions.wrong_if: Real-world invoice batches are flat (no hierarchy) so tree pruning offers zero benefit over linear scan.
inventions.check_note: Predicate over invoice lines with an action, and predicates can relate lines to each other.
inventions.demand: AP team leads in most large organizations oversee mismatch resolution daily, but smaller firms may not have this role.

inventions.name: BisectClaim
inventions.plain: This tool quickly pinpoints the exact moment a medical bill went from looking good to having a problem, like finding a needle in a haystack. Instead of spending weeks hunting through the entire history of a bill, it finds the issue in seconds.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who investigate why a medical claim got rejected or went wrong
inventions.one_line: Uses binary search across a claim's history of status changes to find the exact moment a claim went from approvable to problematic.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: git bisect marks commits as 'good' or 'bad' to find the first bad commit. Mapping: A claim goes through multiple status changes (submitted, partially reviewed, pended, approved, etc.). The model acts as the oracle, answering for each status-change point: 'Would this claim be approvable if we stopped here?' The model examines the claim snapshot at each state (line items, attachments, notes) and returns 'GOOD' (would have been approved), 'BAD' (would be denied), or 'UNCERTAIN' (needs human). API shape: POST /v1/claims/bisect, input claim ID + list of status transition timestamps, output for each timestamp a classification.
inventions.instead_of: Post-claim audit processes that take 2-3 weeks to identify where a claim went wrong. Replaces manual review of 100% of claim history.
inventions.different_because: ClaimCycle shows timeline dashboards; it does not binary-search for inflection points or have a model that decides 'good vs bad' per state.
inventions.better_at: Root-cause identification time: from 14 days to <2 minutes for the median claim error. Measured as 'time from audit start to first bad state identified'.
inventions.price: $0.20 per claim bisection (up to 30 snapshots), $15,000 minimum monthly
inventions.wrong_if: Human auditors reviewing the same claims cannot agree with the model's 'first bad state' in >70% of cases within a 2-state tolerance, showing the oracle is unreliable.
inventions.check_note: Binary search a claim's status history for where it went wrong, with the model as oracle.
inventions.demand: Larger insurance companies regularly split complex claims into parts, but smaller firms do this only occasionally for complicated cases.

inventions.name: PermitContract
inventions.plain: This tool lets you control who can see or change each part of a contract. It stops sensitive information from being accidentally shared with the wrong people.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who share legal documents with others and need to keep certain parts private
inventions.one_line: Assigns access permissions to contract sections so only authorized reviewers can see or edit specific clauses, like chmod for legal documents.
inventions.how_it_works: A = chmod/ACLs set read/write/execute permissions on files for users/groups. Map: model receives a contract and a set of role definitions (e.g., 'finance team: read sections 4.1-4.5, no edit; legal: read+edit all; sales: read only sections 1-3'). The model segments the contract into logical sections (clauses, subclauses, exhibits), assigns each section a permission mask based on the rules, and returns a structured permission map. The model decides section boundaries and handles cross-references (e.g., 'as defined in Section 7.2' grants implicit read). Output: {sections: [{id, text, permissions: {read: [roles], write: [roles]}}]}.
inventions.instead_of: Lawyers emailing contract PDFs with 'please review sections 4-6 only' and relying on trust, leading to 15% of contract leaks according to industry reports.
inventions.different_because: DocuSign allows you to set who can view/sign the whole document, not per section. If a salesperson needs one clause, they get the whole contract.
inventions.better_at: Granularity: clause-level vs document-level; reduce unauthorized access incidents by measured 90% (pre/post deployment audit).
inventions.who_pays: Chief Compliance Officer or VP of Legal at companies with NDAs, M&A documents, or IP-sensitive contracts
inventions.price: Per contract per month: $5 per contract stored (unlimited permission checks)
inventions.wrong_if: A user with permission to read 'Section 5' but not 'Section 6' issues a query and the model reveals content from Section 6 due to a cross-reference in Section 5 that was automatically expanded.
inventions.check_note: Clause-level approval authority. DocuSign permissions the whole document; who may accept an indemnity cap is a different question.
inventions.demand: Organizations of all sizes that deal with NDAs, M&A, or IP contracts need contract review and redlining, making it common across many large industries.

inventions.name: FlakeRank
inventions.plain: It takes all the test failures, groups them by the real reason they failed, and counts how often each problem happens, then shows which tests fail the most. This saves hours of manual sorting and helps focus on fixing the most troublesome tests first.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who manage lots of website tests and spend hours each week trying to figure out which ones are failing and why.
inventions.one_line: Groups E2E test failures by root-cause pattern, counts them, and ranks flakiest tests by failure frequency across runs.
inventions.how_it_works: A = sort | uniq -c: canonicalize test failure messages (normalize timestamps, line numbers, memory addresses), group identical normalized failures, count occurrences across 100+ runs, rank descending. Model decides which failure messages are equivalent (e.g., 'Cannot find element #login' vs 'element #login not found' are same root cause; 'Timeout after 30s waiting for #login' is different). Does not fix, only reports. API: POST /v1/flake-rank with array of run metadata (suite, test name, failure message, timestamp). Returns [{test_name, failure_signature, count, rank}]. Model outputs a yes/no on equivalence pairs.
inventions.instead_of: Manual bucketing of flaky test failures in a spreadsheet (takes 2-4 hours/week for a 50-person team).
inventions.closest_today: Datadog CI Test Visibility flaky test report
inventions.different_because: Datadog groups failures by test name only, not by failure message content. Two different flaky failures in the same test appear as one bucket. Datadog does not canonicalize error messages.
inventions.better_at: Time to identify top-5 flaky root causes across 500 tests/100 runs: from 4 hours to 5 minutes.
inventions.price: $299 per month per 10 repos, unlimited runs
inventions.wrong_if: A competitor (e.g., Launchable, Testim) already releases a 'failure message canonicalization and ranking' feature.
inventions.check_note: Grouping by canonicalised failure signature, not test name. Datadog CI groups by test name only, which is the actual gap.
inventions.demand: QA Managers and DevOps leads in medium-to-large software teams triage flaky tests daily or weekly.

inventions.name: TraceBrowse
inventions.plain: It records every single thing your automated website helper did, with exact times, so you can see exactly where and why it failed. This saves you from guessing what went wrong by looking at blurry screenshots or replaying the whole thing over and over.
inventions.who_it_helps: People whose automated website helpers fail and want to know exactly what happened without guesswork.
inventions.one_line: A full, timestamped trace of every action and system call a browser automation script made, for debugging why it broke.
inventions.how_it_works: A (strace) maps to B: every browser command (click, navigate, extract) and every underlying Playwright/system call (network, DOM fetch, timer) is logged with timestamps and return values into a spool file. The model then analyses the trace to pinpoint the exact failure (e.g., 'selector found element but it was hidden, at t=12.3s, because CSS display:none was set 10ms earlier'). The trace is returned as a JSON array of events; the model can be queried with POST /v1/traces/{id}/analyze to 'whodunnit'. API shape: POST /v1/navigate?trace=true returns trace ID, then GET /v1/traces/{id} or analyze endpoint.
inventions.instead_of: Manual debugging of Playwright/Selenium failures by reading screenshots, logs, and replaying tests.
inventions.better_at: Mean time to diagnose: <30 seconds for the model to output root cause vs. 10+ minutes for a human debugger to read logs and screenshots.
inventions.price: $0.10 per trace with analysis, $300/month minimum
inventions.wrong_if: A bug caused by a race condition that is not visible in any trace (e.g., GPU timing issue) cannot be diagnosed by analyzing syscalls, proving the model's analysis is useless >20% of the time.
inventions.check_note: Playwright Trace Viewer shows the trace but explains nothing. A model reading a trace to name the cause is the missing half.
inventions.demand: QA engineers debugging failed browser tests trace through each step several times a week.

inventions.name: ClauseGuard
inventions.plain: This tool checks contracts against a set of rules to catch mistakes or problems. It saves hours of time and prevents costly errors from being missed.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who review business agreements to make sure they follow company rules
inventions.one_line: Enforces legal policies with declarative rules that accept, flag, or reject contract clauses, like iptables for contract review.
inventions.how_it_works: A = iptables chains rules with conditions (source IP, port) and actions (ACCEPT, DROP, REDIRECT). Map: model accepts a contract clause and a set of user-defined rules. Each rule has a condition (e.g., 'if clause type == indemnification AND scope includes IP infringement') and an action ('allow', 'flag_for_review', 'reject'). The model classifies each clause (type, entities, amounts), evaluates it against the ordered rule chain, and returns the final action plus explanation. Rules can be created/modified by users via a simple DSL (e.g., 'rule: if indemnification.amount > $1M then flag').
inventions.instead_of: Legal operations teams manually checking each contract against a playbook of 20–50 policies, taking 1 hour per contract at $200/hr.
inventions.closest_today: Ironclad Contract Review (AI-powered clause extraction but no custom rule engine)
inventions.different_because: Ironclad extracts predefined clause types but does not let users define conditional logic like 'if clause X AND amount > Y then reject'. Users must manually review extracted clauses.
inventions.better_at: Time to evaluate a 50-page contract against 20 rules: 2 minutes vs 60 minutes; rule processing speed: 1000 clauses/second vs human rate of 1 clause per 30 seconds.
inventions.who_pays: VP of Legal Operations or Procurement Director at companies with >100 contracts/year
inventions.price: $500/month base + $0.50 per contract evaluated
inventions.wrong_if: A rule says 'reject all clauses with liability cap below $1M', but the model lets through a clause with cap at $500k because it misreads '$500,000' as '$500,000,000'.
inventions.check_note: A standing ordered playbook with a default policy, distinct from W038's ad-hoc query. Ironclad extracts predefined types and cannot express a chain.
inventions.demand: Companies that process more than 100 contracts per year regularly spend on contract review and redlining in their legal or procurement departments.

inventions.name: DocTables
inventions.plain: This tool lets you set up simple rules that automatically sort, approve, or reject documents based on what they say or what they are. It saves people from having to decide and click on every single document one by one.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to route many documents to different places based on their content
inventions.one_line: Declare rule chains that accept, flag, or redirect documents based on content and metadata.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: iptables chains have rules with matches and targets (ACCEPT, DROP, REDIRECT). Model evaluates each doc against a chain of rules. Model decides if a rule's condition (e.g., 'contains trade secret phrase') is satisfied, then executes target: ACCEPT (allow to review), DROP (exclude), REDIRECT (tag and send to another chain). API shape: POST /v1/doctables with chain definition; model returns action per doc.
inventions.instead_of: Manual coding of each document with no automated branching logic.
inventions.closest_today: Brainspace's active learning (flat yes/no classification, no chaining).
inventions.different_because: Brainspace cannot chain 'if privileged then redact, else if confidential then restrict access, else allow' in one pass.
inventions.better_at: Review accuracy improves by 30% (fewer misclassifications) due to explicit rule chaining.
inventions.price: $0.30 per 1,000 docs processed, $2,000 monthly minimum
inventions.wrong_if: A doc that should be flagged 'privileged' is dropped because rule chain misorders conditions.
inventions.check_note: Chain 'if privileged then redact then route'. Privilege review is the expensive part and Brainspace cannot express a chain.
inventions.demand: Compliance officers in regulated industries (finance, healthcare) regularly oversee document review for audits and investigations.

inventions.name: ModalReview
inventions.plain: It lets workers make decisions on financial background checks by picking steps from a simple menu, instead of clicking lots of buttons. This saves workers from having to click 15 or more times for each decision they make.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who review financial background checks and want to make decisions faster without all the clicking.
inventions.one_line: Modal grammar interface for KYC case review where analysts compose operations from finite operator-motion-object slots
inventions.how_it_works: A = vim's modal editing: different modes (normal, insert, visual) with operators (d, y, c) + motions (w, b, j) + objects (w, s, p). Map: Review modes = Scan (read-only), Investigate (dig into fields), Document (add notes). Operators = flag, escalate, approve, request_info. Motions = next_field, prev_case, jump_to_entity. Objects = transaction, address, ID_document. Model translates keystroke sequences into case actions. API: POST /v1/case/command with {case_id, mode, operator, motion, object}. Model resolves ambiguous commands (e.g., 'delete' in review context = 'remove from queue' not 'delete data').
inventions.instead_of: Mouse-driven KYC review tools (e.g., LexisNexis Bridger) requiring 15+ clicks per decision
inventions.different_because: Bridger XG is a point-and-click web app. ModalReview is a keyboard-driven modal interface where analysts compose operations without lifting hands from keyboard, with model disambiguating intent from context.
inventions.better_at: Actions per minute: 4 clicks/min in Bridger → 12 command sequences/min in ModalReview (3x). Error rate: 8% → 2% due to constrained command set.
inventions.price: $3,000/user/year, 50-user minimum
inventions.wrong_if: Analysts reject keyboard-driven workflow and revert to mouse within 2 weeks, showing no productivity gain
inventions.check_note: Modal dispositioning for analysts making the same few decisions thousands of times. Bridger XG is point-and-click.
inventions.demand: Heads of financial crime operations use this for KYC and AML case review, a regular job in many financial firms.

inventions.name: SED-Case
inventions.plain: It quickly hides private information in financial reports and creates a clean copy ready for regulators. This saves workers from spending 45 minutes and $150 per report manually blacking out details.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to remove personal details from financial reports before sending them to regulators.
inventions.one_line: Regex-based case redaction and substitution engine for KYC/AML documents that produces regulator-ready audit trails
inventions.how_it_works: A = sed's s/pattern/replacement/flags applied to lines. Map: each KYC field (name, address, account) is a 'line' token. The model applies sed-like substitutions but with semantic pattern matching (e.g., 'replace all mentions of person X in narrative fields' where model identifies entity boundaries). API shape: POST /v1/case/redact with {case_id, rules: [{pattern: 'entity_type:person:John Doe', replacement: '[REDACTED]', flags: 'g'}]}. Model decides entity boundaries and whether substitution would break document meaning, returning 'ambiguous' if unsure.
inventions.instead_of: Manual analyst redaction at $150/hour taking 45 minutes per case
inventions.different_because: OneTrust uses ML classification to find PII then applies blanket redaction. SED-Case lets analysts write composable pattern rules (e.g., 'redact all accounts opened before 2020 except if flagged') and the model applies them with context awareness, not just regex or ML tags.
inventions.better_at: Redaction speed: 45 minutes → 90 seconds per case, 30x faster. Audit trail completeness: every substitution logged with before/after and model confidence score.
inventions.price: $5,000/month per 1,000 cases, tiered at $4/case after 10,000
inventions.wrong_if: An analyst can manually redact a case faster than the model + review time combined for any case type
inventions.check_note: Rule-driven redaction and substitution with a reviewable rule, against OneTrust's classify-then-act pipeline.
inventions.demand: Heads of financial crime operations use this for KYC and AML case review, a routine need across financial institutions.

inventions.name: MakeCase
inventions.plain: It lets you set up rules like 'finish this check before moving to the next one,' and only redoes the steps that need updating when something changes. This saves people from having to redo all steps by hand, which takes nearly an hour.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who need to run a series of checks in a specific order and don't want to restart everything when one thing changes
inventions.one_line: Declares KYC case resolution dependencies (e.g., 'document check must pass before screening') and rebuilds only stale sub-tasks when a source changes.
inventions.how_it_works: make maps to case resolution workflows. Analysts declare targets (e.g., 'approve' with dependencies ['doc_check', 'screen']) and rules. API: POST /v1/cases/build with {case_id, targets: ['approve']}. Model checks timestamps of each sub-task result and decides which are stale (e.g., source data changed). Returns {stale_tasks: [doc_check], rebuilt_results: {...}}. Only stale tasks execute.
inventions.instead_of: Manual re-run of all checks (6 steps) when one source changes, taking 45 minutes.
inventions.different_because: Fenergo has fixed sequential workflows but no dependency graph or stale detection. It can't skip completed steps.
inventions.better_at: Re-resolution time when source changes: from 45 minutes to 5 minutes (9x faster).
inventions.price: $10 per build, or $1,000/month flat for unlimited builds.
inventions.wrong_if: If a change in a source document requires re-running a sub-task that makeCase marks as fresh, the dependency model is wrong.
inventions.check_note: Dependency-aware case resolution; Fenergo's workflow is a fixed sequence.
inventions.demand: Compliance engineers build and adjust case rules regularly at larger banks.

inventions.name: AwkMatch
inventions.plain: It reads numbers and details from each bill and puts them into the right spots automatically. This saves someone from having to type all that information by hand from hundreds of bills every day.
inventions.who_it_helps: people who have to copy information from lots of printed or digital bills into a computer
inventions.one_line: Extract and transform fields from each invoice line automatically, using pattern-action rules written by the model.
inventions.how_it_works: An awk-inspired pipeline: for each line in an invoice, the model assigns a pattern (regex or field position) and an action (extract, transform, flag). The API shape is POST /v1/patterns with {pattern, action}. For example, vendor names are field 1, amounts field 3 with currency stripping. The model examines one correction and writes the awk program. Human validates the pattern. Batched execution on all future invoices.
inventions.instead_of: Clerks manually copying vendor, date, amount from 200 PDF invoices daily.
inventions.closest_today: Rossum's AI field extraction requires 50+ training documents per template.
inventions.different_because: Rossum needs bulk training. AwkMatch writes a pattern from a single correction, like awk -F',' 'print $1' from one example.
inventions.better_at: Setup time per new vendor: 1 correction vs. 50 training documents (10x faster).
inventions.price: $0.10 per pattern evaluation, minimum $200/month.
inventions.wrong_if: If invoice layouts are too variable (e.g., field order changes per vendor), AwkMatch patterns break more than 30% of the time without human re-validation.
inventions.check_note: Write one pattern-action rule instead of training an extractor per layout.
inventions.demand: AP specialists in many mid-to-large companies deal with invoice exceptions regularly, but it's one task among several.

inventions.name: AlertChain
inventions.plain: It lets you set up simple 'if this happens, then do that' rules for how to handle computer warnings. The rules are checked in a strict order, so every warning gets treated the same way every time.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to decide what to do with each computer warning using only their memory
inventions.one_line: Declares chains of if-this-then-that rules that accept, escalate, or suppress alerts, evaluated in priority order like a firewall ruleset.
inventions.how_it_works: Analysts write declarative rules: e.g., `RULE 1: if severity >= 8 then ESCALATE; RULE 2: if source_ip in ['10.0.0.0/8'] then ACCEPT; RULE 3: if alert_name contains 'scanner' and count_per_hour > 100 then DROP`. Every incoming alert is evaluated against the chain in order; the first matching rule's action (ACCEPT/ESCALATE/DROP/REDIRECT) is taken. The model only decides whether an alert's fields match a rule's condition—no complex reasoning. API shape: POST /v1/alerts/chain with body {'rules': [...], 'alert': {...}} returns {'action': 'drop', 'matched_rule': 'RULE 3', 'reason': 'scanner > 100/hr'}.
inventions.instead_of: The current practice of analysts evaluating each alert against mental heuristics with no enforced priority order.
inventions.different_because: XSOAR playbooks are multi-step automation workflows with conditions, actions, and branches; they are not a simple, flat, priority-ordered chain of accept/drop/redirect rules evaluated statelessly per alert.
inventions.better_at: Rule evaluation latency: AlertChain processes 10,000 alerts/second per chain (~0.1ms per alert) vs. XSOAR playbook execution which averages 500ms per alert.
inventions.price: $200 per chain (rule group) per month; up to 5 chains included.
inventions.wrong_if: If a controlled test shows more than 5% of alerts misrouted due to rule order conflicts that an analyst could not have predicted.
inventions.check_note: A lightweight ordered rule chain with semantic matches and a default policy, against XSOAR's heavyweight playbooks. Same mechanism family as Z010 but a different domain, buyer and price point.
inventions.demand: SOC engineers often chain multiple alert investigations together when dealing with complex incidents.

inventions.name: AlertPatch
inventions.plain: It compares today's batch of warnings to yesterday's and automatically applies the same decision to matching ones. This stops you from having to decide the same thing over and over again for the same problem.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who have to decide what to do about the same warning alert, hour after hour, for days.
inventions.one_line: Computes the minimal change between a current alert batch and the previous one, then auto-applies the triage decision from the prior match.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: diff computes line-level changes; patch applies them. B's mapping: AlertPatch takes the current 100-alert batch and the previous batch, diffs the alert_id + feature vectors (IPs, hashes, ports). Where diff says 'same cluster as prior solved alert X', it auto-applies the prior analyst decision (e.g., 'No action - malware was cleared'). The model decides which alert pairs are 'semantically equivalent' by comparing embedding cosine distance against a threshold.
inventions.instead_of: Analysts re-triaging the same log4j pattern every 4 hours for 3 weeks. Manual repetition costs $400/hr wasted.
inventions.different_because: Splunk dedup is exact field match (same src_ip, same rule). AlertPatch uses learned embeddings to catch 'same attack, different destination ports' and auto-apply the old verdict.
inventions.better_at: Time to triage identical-attack resurgence: from 30 minutes per analyst -> 0 seconds (auto-resolved). Reduces repeat handling by 80%.
inventions.price: $0.02 per patch (auto-resolution) with a cap of $20k/month per team.
inventions.wrong_if: If in a 30-day pilot, >30% of auto-patched alerts are later found to have been mis-classified (analyst must reverse).
inventions.check_note: Semantic alert deduplication. Splunk notable-event dedup is exact field match, so the same attack in a different shape arrives twice.
inventions.demand: Mid-to-large companies with a security operations center have analysts review security alerts frequently, though only a minority of all organizations run a SOC.

inventions.name: GrepTest
inventions.plain: It looks at a log of what happened during a test and picks out only the important checkpoints that failed, so you don't have to run the entire test again. This saves time and computer power by focusing only on the bits that matter.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who run lots of website tests and waste time rerunning them just to see if a single thing went wrong.
inventions.one_line: Stream-matching test runner: grep relevant assertions from a running test log, not replay the whole suite.
inventions.how_it_works: Maps grep's stream+matching: test execution emits a live log stream. The model watches for patterns like error codes, diff output, or performance regressions. API: POST /v1/test/match with {stream_id, pattern: "FAIL|error|slow"} returns {matched_chunks: ["..."], line_numbers}. The model decides if a pattern indicates a real failure vs. flaky noise, then emits a 'hit' to stop or flag. No healing—just exact pattern matching plus judgement.
inventions.instead_of: Flaky test rerun systems (e.g., Test Retry in Cypress) that waste compute on full re-execution
inventions.better_at: Test time per flaky detection: from ~30 seconds per rerun (full test) to <2 seconds for pattern match on stream, 15x faster.
inventions.price: Per-match: $0.001 per pattern check, $100/month for 100k checks
inventions.wrong_if: A flaky test emits a false-positive pattern that passes the LLM judgement, causing a production bug to be missed.
inventions.check_note: Model-driven triage of a live test log, so a flaky failure is classified without a rerun. Reruns are the cost being attacked.
inventions.demand: Engineering managers and DevOps in tech companies periodically grep logs to diagnose test failures, often weekly.

inventions.name: PatchFlow
inventions.plain: It figures out the smallest changes between two pages and clicks through the steps to get from one to the other. This means you don't have to teach it every single click or rewrite instructions when things shift slightly.
inventions.who_it_helps: People who need to walk through a website step by step but hate re-recording everything when the site updates.
inventions.one_line: Compute the minimal change set between two page states and apply it as a navigational patch.
inventions.how_it_works: A's design: diff computes minimal edits to transform file A into file B; patch applies them to a third file. Mapping: Given two DOM snapshots (before/after navigation), the model computes a minimal set of CSS selector + action tuples (click X, type Y, wait for Z) that transforms the 'before' DOM into the 'after' DOM. Patch applies these actions to a new page with a similar but not identical DOM. API shape: POST /v1/patchflow/diff { before_html, after_html } returns actions[]. POST /v1/patchflow/apply { target_html, actions } returns result html.
inventions.instead_of: Step-recording tools (Katalon, Selenium IDE) that capture brittle coordinates; manual scripting of each page interaction.
inventions.better_at: Patch succeeds on 85% of structurally similar pages vs. 20% for recorded coordinates; reduces test maintenance from 5 hours/week to 30 minutes/week.
inventions.who_pays: QA Engineering Manager or Web Scraping Team Lead
inventions.price: $0.05 per diff, $0.10 per apply; volume discounts at 10K/month = $700
inventions.wrong_if: If on 50 production pages, the patch fails more than 15% of the time when the target page has <=10% DOM structural difference from source.
inventions.check_note: Structural diff between two DOM snapshots as the repair signal, rather than re-guessing a selector. Distinct from healing: it computes what changed instead of searching for a substitute.
inventions.demand: QA and web scraping teams at e-commerce and data companies patch broken browser scripts a few times per week.
